23500: Myogenic heterochronies have not been studied in anurans. Xenopus laevis exhibits muscle function prior to multinucleation of axial myotome. It is interesting to determine if the early muscle function in X. laevis is a heterochronic event shared with other pipids or a unique trait of X. laevis. Herein, we studied myogenesis in the pipid Hymenochirus boettgeri. We specifically focused on the timing of four events: 1) initial presence of muscle protein, 2) first stimulated twitch, 3) first spontaneous twitch, and 4) onset of multinucleation. Muscle protein was detected at stage 25 (Nieuwkoop and Faber, 1956, developmental table for Xenopus) using the 12/101 anti-muscle antibody and the DAB substrate reaction. Muscle was stimulated with a metal probe and observations were made under a dissecting microscope. Stimulated first twitch took place by stages 27/28, whereas spontaneous twitch occurred at stage 31. Methacrylate sections stained with toluidine blue revealed multinucleated myotome after stage 42. Overall, myogenic events in H. boettgeri occur in the same sequence as in X. laevis, but delayed by 2-3 stages, except multinucleation, which occurs around the same stage in both species. In addition, first heartbeat is also delayed in H. boettgeri (stage 36/37, compared to 33/34 in X. laevis).

23501: Aroclor® 1242 is a polychlorinated biphenyl (PCB) formulation reported to have endocrine disrupting activity in many animals. To examine its effects on amphibian metamorphosis, tadpoles resulting from two morphologically disparate egg masses were orally dosed daily throughout the larval period, approximately eight months. The effects on ranid metamorphosis varied between the egg masses. In the first egg mass, tentatively identified as R. sphenocephala, there was no statistical difference between treatments in the number of metamorphs at the end of the experiment. In the second egg mass, tentatively identified as R. palustris, PCB treatment was correlated with an increase in the number of tadpoles completing metamorphosis, significantly in the highest dose. The apparent stimulation of metamorphosis in the second egg mass by PCB exposure may be due to an endocrine disrupting effect on the corticosterone "stress" axis. A thyroid-mediated mechanism of effect is also possible. The increase in metamorphosis in the PCB treated groups was only significant at the highest dose (1000 pg/g). This level of contamination exceeds concentrations likely to occur in the wild. Based upon these results, it is unlikely that PCB exposure in the wild is altering time to metamorphosis to a degree that would detrimentally effect amphibian populations. Interpretation of these results is hampered by the difficulty in identifying the ranid larvae. Efforts are ongoing to resolve the identification of the tadpoles and froglets.
Virginia Institute of Marine Science, College of William and Mary, Gloucester Point, VA 23062 USA
23502: A population of the wood turtle (Clemmys insculpta) was studied in the Moordener Kill, Rensselear County, New York from May 18 to November 5, 1997. All captures and data was collected from turtles found in the stream or basking in a position to be visible from the stream. Sixty-one captures resulting in a total of 18 adults (10 males and 8 females) and eight juveniles captured. Each individual was measured and marked. Ages ranged from two to indistinguishable. Sexual maturity was attained at age eleven in this population. The mean carapace length of ten adult males was 183.7 mm, with the maximum being 195 mm in a male that was over twenty years of age. No individual was found with a body mass greater than 950 grams. This is a smaller body size than has been recorded in many southern populations of Clemmys insculpta that have been studied. Water temperature was recorded at the time of capture. A negative correlation was recorded for body mass and coldest water at capture for each individual (r= -0.485). No turtle smaller than 725 grams was captured after the water temperature dropped below 11 degrees Celsius. All turtle activity stopped when the water temperature reached 7 degrees celsius.

23503: From June to October 1994, we used five drift fences, 20 m-long with 10 pitfall traps each side, to sample migrating red efts (Notophthalmus viridescens) in terrestrial habitats near Lake Lafond in the Mastigouche Reserve, Quebec. Fences were at varying distances (up to 200 m) from the shore. Eft age was estimated by skeletochronology. More than 1200 specimens, from a total of 1443, were the smallest (mean SVL = 21.5 mm) and youngest efts (0+, 1 and 2 yr) caught while migrating towards the forest; most of these (83%) were caught in fences A and C, at 15 m from the shore, between 7 and 30 September. The 226 efts caught migrating towards the lake were more frequent (81.6%) in June and August. The ones caught in fences A, B and C (up to 87 m from the shore) were maturing efts with mean SVL of 32.3 mm (max: 39) and aged between 3 and 5 yr. The adult newt population in Lake Lafond was known to have a modal age frequency of 4 yr and a maximum age of 10 yr. It is concluded for this population that the terrestrial eft stage lasts a maximum of 5 yr, that maturity can be reached at 3 yr in both sexes, and that females tend to be larger than males at specific ages.

23504: Changes in head size and shape during development occur in all vertebrates. One general observation is that the eyes of most vertebrates are large early in development and that the remainder of the head tends to grow around them. This paper presents a comparative study of the relative size and position of the eyes within and among different groups of snakes. Of particular interest are changes associated with head size in left and right visual field overlap, with respect to both quantity and direction of overlap. For example, in some arboreal species, the eyes are rotated about the dorsal-ventral axis towards the frontal plane during ontogeny. This increases the frontal binocular overlap, while sacrificing some of the postero-lateral visual field. These changes may be the consequence of structural changes to increase gape and the development of larger, more powerful jaw musculature in larger individuals for capturing and ingesting larger prey. Correlations with natural history and phylogeny are discussed together with some hypotheses of ultimate causation.

23505: Rommy has completed his Ph.D. degree at a well-known university. He can't find a job. After a series of postdoctoral positions he comes to Canada for yet another bout of training. After learning how to gather molecular data he begins the analysis. He encounters a strange philosophy for reconstructing genealogical associations, one that seems to conflict with his previous training. Although he considers himself a cladist, it seems he knows virtually nothing about the history of systematics and the assumptions behind various methods of analysis. He doesn't even understand the basic difference between phenetics and cladistics, or why Neighbor-joining phenograms conflict with parsimony analyses, why maximum likelihood estimates of phylogeny fail, and why frequency data suck. As the pressure to publish his data mounts, he suffers the wrath of reviewers and editors who have their own vested interests to defend. He eventually figures out that a philosophy underlying a methodology is important, then realizes that even this - and all the petty squabbeling over it -- is trivial...

23506: The lake chub (Couesius plumbeus), the most widespread minnow in northern North America, ranges from Alaska to New England. Couesius is regarded as monotypic, but its relationships have been debated and there have been questions as to whether or not the species is polytypic. Several recent studies cited in the literature remain unpublished. In 1941, Hubbs and Lagler reported that two subspecies, occasionally sympatric though usually separated ecologically, occurred on the Keweenaw Peninsula. Later these authors suggested that the two forms verged on full specific distinction. Restudy of their abundant material supplemented by new collections indicates that there are, in fact, two morphs of the lake chub in the area, one chiefly in creeks, the other in Lake Superior shorewaters and rivermouths. The creek form has a smaller eye, a shorter and slightly more rounded dorsal fin, and significantly fewer vertebrae. I suggest that these reflect different ecological conditions during development. Downstream drift of creek fish has resulted in sympatry of the lake and creek morphs at the mouth of Eagle River. The relationships of Couesius are discussed.

23507: Surface fresh waters represent 0.01% of the planet's water, of which 1% was in rivers, 99% in lakes. Now reservoirs hold five times as much water as river beds and affect flow seasonality. Agriculture severely affects fish habitat by water withdrawal and quality of runoff. Biological (exotics) and industrial chemical pollution also affect ecosystem integrity. Freshwater fishes comprise 40.4% of the world's fish species. Freshwater fish diversity is unevenly distributed. Polar and arid areas have few species, rivers more than lakes. Six countries, Brazil, Indonesia, China, Zaire, Peru and U.S., contain over 90% of freshwater fish species. Species geographic density, rather than absolute counts, provides a different country list. Equal-area geographic grids offer a superior method of identifying biodiversity hotspots. Globally about 20% of the world's freshwater fish species are extinct, endangered, or vulnerable. Numerous productive fisheries are at risk. Driving forces, not just immediate human impacts need to be considered. 54% of the planet's accessible runoff is now used in growing human populations. Present economic frameworks are reducing capacity of governments to respond. Serious responses need to be initiated before the new millennium if the collision between needs of humans and freshwater biota does not result in massive extinctions.

23508: A distinctive form of longnose sucker, the Salish sucker, occurs in southwestern British Columbia and western Washington. Salish suckers differ from other western longnose suckers in both their morphometry and mitochondrial genome. Thus, both morphometric and molecular data indicate that Salish suckers have diverged from other northwestern longnose suckers; however, our molecular data suggests an even 'deeper' divergence between western and eastern longnose suckers, and the Salish sucker is unambiguously part of the western lineage. This implies that the Salish sucker evolved after the divergence of western and eastern longnose suckers. The geographic distribution of Salish suckers is consistent with a pre-Wisconscinan origin south of Puget Sound and post glacial dispersal north into southwestern B.C. The Salish sucker is in decline throughout its geographic range and probably will be extinct in southwestern B.C. within a decade. The diagnostic mitochondrial haplotypes characteristics of the Salish sucker argue that a unique part of the evolutionary history of the longnose sucker will be lost with the extinction of the Salish sucker. As such they constitute and Evolutionarily Significant Unit and warrant some protection in Washington State where there still is at least one large population.

23509: Muskellunge, the largest freshwater sports species in temperate North America, are venerable fish whose size and stature match those of their benefactor, Dr. E. J. Crossman. Naturally sustaining muskellunge populations that produce 'trophy' fish are a valuable resource. Dr. Crossman's studies over the years have provided a legacy essential to our understanding of the species' biology and its management. We review the relationship between length of the researcher and that of the fish studied. Was there a natural affinity here? Dr. Crossman has encouraged acquisition and archiving of biological data on this relatively rare fish, so where once there was little, now there is a wealth of information to manage and assess exploitation. Using the Cleithrum Project archive, we developed a precise, biologically based method for setting size limits that guarantees adequate reproductive capacity and determines a Minimum Ultimate (trophy) Size Limit (M.U.S.L.) based on comparable growth potential for male and female muskellunge from 14 Ontario sources, we demonstrate how data on as few as 11 fish (>8 -11 yr.) can adequately describe growth potential. Age and number of muskellunge that exceed M.S.U. can indicate how well we perpetuate the legacy of good science and rational, conservative management encouraged by Ed.

23510: In his direction to students, Dr. E.J. Crossman emphasizes and encourages a comprehensive approach to questions and problems of fish systematic and taxonomic studies which, at the time I was doing my degree work, were dominated by morphological and osetological approaches. Recently such studies have become dominated by genetic approaches which often rely solely upon tissues provided to laboratories rather than the fish themselves, and focus solely upon variation at the molecular level. Little or no reference is usually made to other character systems such as morphology, osteology, ecology or biology. For well known groups and studies at higher taxonomic levels this bias may not matter, and genetic studies add another dimension to our knowledge. However, for poorly known groups and lower taxonomic levels, working solely with tissues can limit understanding, may bias results, and result in erroneous conclusions. External morphology is often the first clue to undiscovered diversity. Genetic variation may be present but without associated knowledge of morphology may not be interpreted correctly. Thus, quantifying and understanding morphological diversity is important in the development of hypotheses which can then be tested using other approaches such as genetics. Morphological diversity within an esociform (Olympic mudminnow, Novumbra hubbsi) and morphological and genetic diversity within a salmoniform group (Arctic and Dolly Varden chars, Salvelinus spp.) are used to illustrate the need for close association of various approaches to achieve fuller understanding of diversity and relationships of fishes. In keeping with the legacy of Dr. Crossman, I advocate a more comprehensive approach to systematic and taxonomic studies which should include reference to morphological, ecological and biological chararactes as well as genetic characters.

23511: We quantified individual differences in reproductive behaviour of Atlantic cod under simulated natural conditions. At field spawning densities, 16 individually marked cod (7 males, 9 females) were observed twice daily and videotaped continuously for 9 weeks at ambient photoperiod and temperature in a large tank. Males established an aggression-based dominance hierarchy with 96% of all agonistic interactions being initiated by the 3 largest males. Microsatellite DNA analysis of 1 female's brood identified paternal gene contributions from the 3 behaviourally dominant males. Interactions between sexes were dominated by male circling of females. After descending to the bottom, a motionless female was circled an average 2.4 times (range: 1 to 11), usually by 1 male per circling bout but by several males throughout the spawning period. Circling may provide opportunities for males to gain individual access to reproductive females and for females to assess the quality of potential mates. Given the prevalence of sound communication among reproductive cod and other gadids, sexual differences in the size of sound-producing muscles in haddock provide indirect evidence of mate choice. The mating conditions of cod and haddock are consistent with the hypothesis that these fish reproduce in leks.

23512: Dr. E. J. Crossman has shown a concern for the biodiversity and decline of fishes in Canada. He is a member of the board on both the national and provincial committees concerned with listing vulnerable, threatened and endangered fishes. He received a grant and coordinated the production of several status reports for the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada. Recently he has become involved in the Committee on the Status of Species at Risk in Ontario. The information which he has helped to produce is used by fishery managers and biological consultants that are attempting to protect habitats and the fishes which are sensitive to its degradation. 23513: In 1993, a joint Royal Ontario Museum - Zoological Institute of St. Petersburg expedition surveyed the fish fauna of Khanka Lake, Russia. Khanka Lake is located on the Russian-Chinese border in the Amur River basin of eastern Asia. It supports a large commercial fishery and its shores are ringed with rice paddies and fish farms. The lake contains a biogeographically interesting fish assemblage with endemic, Eurasian, Manchurian, and Sino-Indian affinities. Historically, the lake has the most diverse fish fauna of any lake in Russia with more than 50 species caught in the lake. The 1993 survey sampled fishes at over 100 sites in Khanka Lake and caught only 34 species. The biological diversity of Khanka Lake appears to be seriously threatened by unregulated overharvesting and cultural eutrophication.

23514: The need for better understanding of the changes in the biodiversity of the fishes of the Great Lakes includes the need to inventory the number of fishes introduced and those which become extirpated. Compiling records on introduced fishes, the lakes they are found in, the vectors used, and their current reproductive status provides valuable information for the monitoring of the fish communities. There have been 52 introduced fishes recorded from the lakes, 27 of which are currently established. It is important to continue to compile this information to track introduced species, not just their arrival, but their establishment and spread, as these species are often referred to as one of the main reasons for changes in the biodiversity of the lakes. Another change to biodiversity is the loss of species. To date, there have been 26 species and subspecies extirpated from one or more of the lakes. Lake Ontario has the highest number of extirpated species, while Lakes Nipigon and Superior have lost no species. Understanding the present fish community and the changes it has experienced, allow for more effective management of the Great Lakes.

23515: The First Graduate Student was sometimes hyperbolic in speech and actions, and his perceptions of the world were spawned at the edge of a cornfield in central Illinois. The Major Professor was different - he never has had a firm grasp on the concept of hyperbole, and he viewed the world through glasses made near some large river in southern Ohio. How, when, and why did they meet? What happened? How could their interactions have formed the foundations for the entire career of The Student? I think I know the answers to these and other questions. I will spend 30 min. on a chronicle of how I met Ron Brandon, the three academic years that I spent in his association when he was a doctoral student at the University of Illinois and I was an undergraduate, and the two years I spent as his first graduate student at Southern Illinois University. I will then add a smattering of happenings since those times. In the process, I hope to illustrate who he is, or who I think he is, and then I will end with a summary - that could be the fun part, because we seldom pause long enough to say "Thank you."

23516: To the degree that a failing memory permits, the presentation will first recount my initial experiences with Dr. Brandon, in Bearcamp Gorge in the summer of 1962, particularly the memorable night of July 4. The important contributions of Dr. Brandon to our understanding of the systematics of Gyrinophilus will then be reviewed. The presentation will conclude with an examination of the current status of our knowledge of Gyrinophilus porphyriticus in the southern Blue Ridge. Patterns of variation in pigmentation, body size, and life history suggest the presence of three geographic variants. Preliminary research has suggested some level of reproductive isolation among at least two of them. Additional genetic and behavioral studies are needed to resolve questions of diversification and speciation in the southern Blue Ridge complex of Gyrinophilus porphyriticus.

23517: In 1976 James Huheey used a functional feeding model to simulate the effects of adding weaker models to simple Mullerian Mimicry system. Huheey concluded that weaker models decrease the survivorship of the stronger models and have the same impact on the models as would Batesian mimics. This conclusion contradicts a number of earlier theoretical and logical assertions, but has apparently survived the test of time rather well. I used a similar functional model of feeding to ask whether specific changes alter the conclusion that Mullerian Mimicry cannot exist. The newer feeding model included both positive and negative values for noxiousness and a wide range of relative proportions of model species. Individuals of the second mimic species were ADDED to a resident pool of noxious model instead of replacing them. This modification was added because models and mimics only share their appearance not necessarily their ecological space. Success, or lack of success, was measured in terms of mortality rates for both species. Results of the simulations delineate situations with "viable" proportions of "models" and "mimics". In all situations where the second species was at all noxious, overall survivorship for the original species increased. Mullerian co-models have exactly the impact that Fisher suggested in 1930. The model used extended the ranges of possible attractiveness beyond the usual limited range of palatable vs. unpalatable and suggests ways of incorporating these variables into more general systems.
Department of Biology, Appalachian State University, Boone, NC 28608, USA
23518: Unmated female smooth newts collected in terrestrial situations were mated in the laboratory, and the ultrastructure of the transferred sperm and the spermathecae was observed at various intervals after mating. Sperm from a spermatophore cap lodged in a female's cloacal orifice can migrate into spermathecae within one hour after mating. Spherical structures on the axial fibers of some sperm in the cap could indicate immaturity. Disorderly clusters of sperm from the cap are still present in the cloacal chamber 12 hours after mating but are absent 24 hours after mating. During storage, sperm often are in tangled masses in the spermathecal tubules. The sperm are coated with spermathecal secretions, and some sperm nuclei were observed embedded in the spermathecal epithelium. Little evidence for spermiophagy early in the breeding season was found. During oviposition, mazes of sperm occur external to the spermathecal orifices, and sperm may be released in this condition onto eggs as they pass through the cloaca. The tangled clusters in which sperm are found from pick-up to oviposition is hypothesized as an adaptation to reduce the effectiveness of sperm competition from the ejaculates of rival males.

23519: Spermatophores of Ambystoma texanum collected in the field from Macoupin and Jackson Counties, Illinois, consist of a sperm filled cap supported by a gelatinous base. This structure is consistent with prior reports for this and other Ambystoma species. Multiple structures consisted of up to 7 spermatophores stacked vertically. Individual spermatophores within multiple structures have a morphology consistent with single spermatophores. Spermatophores within multiple structures adhere to each other. The base of each stacked spermatophore typically covers the subjacent spermatophore cap, leaving only the cap of the top spermatophore exposed. Five spermatophore fields of 21-535 spermatophores were examined. The percent of spermatophores in multiple structures was positively correlated with the number of spermatophores within a spermatophore field (19%, N = 21; 73.8%, N = 112-120; 83.7%, N = 378-535 spermatophores). Further, the number of spermatophores within multiple structures was positively correlated with the number of spermatophores within a spermatophore field (22% of all spermatophores were in structures of 4 or more spermatophores for N = 378-535; 15.7% for N= 112-120; and 0% for N = 21 spermatophores).
23520: Field experiences, from cave bottoms to mountaintops, from the swamps of Southern Illinois to the balds and rain forests of the Blue Ridge and Smoky Mountains, will be discussed. Along the way, previously undescribed forms have been described, studied, and also overlooked. Rare species were sometime plentiful, and "common" species unobtainable. Mimics changed from Batesian to Mullerian. And a good time was had by all.

23521: Although the paedomorphic salamanders Ambystoma mexicanum and Ambystoma dumerilii are not known to metamorphose in nature they often undergo spontaneous metamorphic changes when maintained in the laboratory. In addition, individuals of these species have been induced to transform with treatments of thyroxin. Descriptions of these transformed individuals are based entirely on external features associated with metamorphosis of the gills and tail fin and variation in these external features indicates that many of the transformed individuals are only partially transformed. This study examines the internal changes that occur in the cranium and hyobranchial apparatus in these species in both spontaneous and induced individuals. The degree of metamorphosis in these individuals is evaluated relative the normal transformations known for metamorphosing sister species and spontaneous and induced changes are compared. Interestingly, most of these transformed individuals, whether metamorphosis is spontaneous or induced, die within 5 months of the onset of transformation. Functional interpretations of the internal anatomical patterns are used to examine the possibility that abnormal metamorphosis limits the feeding ability of these individuals, thus, contributing to their short term post "metamorphic" survival.

23522: The Mexican ambystomatid salamanders comprise a group of about 15 species, all of which are part of the tiger salamander (Ambystoma tigrinum) complex. The paedomorphic populations from Puebla and adjacent Veracruz were originally brought to our attention by Ron Brandon, and constitute a system of extraordinary interest for the study of speciation and the evolution of metamorphosis. The region contains at least five lacustrine, paedomorphic populations which demonstrate a wide range of morphological and physiological novelties, while the metamorphosing animals from the same region appear to fall within the limits of normal A. velasci. Based on both allozyme and mitochondrial DNA sequence data, most of these taxa are virtually indistinguishable, suggesting that the ambystomatid radiation from the Puebla lakes region has taken place in the very recent past. As such, it constitutes an example of very rapid physiological and morphological evolution, and possible speciation, as well as severe conservation challenges to preserve these narrowly restricted taxa.

23523: Several important geophysical trends in Mexico and Central America are reflected in the pattern of relationships among lizards of the genus Ctenosaura. The spiny-tailed iguanas are primarily lowland species whose current distributions appear to have been influenced by both fragmentation and dispersal. Identifiable events cluster into one of two general categories which include those which are fairly recent (< 3 mya) or those which are relatively older (> 5 mya). Species or species groups whose divergences reflect relatively older events may have resulted from uplift of interior highlands, isolation of the Baja peninsula and previous isolation of Lower Central America from Nuclear Central America and Mexico. More recently diverged species may be the result of episodes such as the emergence of the isthmus of Tehuantepec, the formation of the Mexican transvolcanics, the fragmentation of Pacific coastal arid habitats and isolation on islands.

23524: Recognizing Desmognathus ocoee as a distinct species is consistent with cladistic and distance analyses of allozyme polymorphisms, but conceals complex patterns of genetic differentiation and significant gaps in our understanding. One difficulty has been our lack of knowledge of the contact zones between D. ocoee and two related taxa; Desmognathus carolinensis in the Blue Ridge and D. ochrophaeus in the Cumberland Plateau. We present data suggesting that the D. ocoee-D. carolinensis "contact zone" is tens of kilometers wide and characterized by discordant variation among several allozyme loci. The Cumberland Plateau populations of D. ocoee are replaced north of the Tennessee River by a form that is strongly differentiated from both D. ocoee and D. ochrophaeus and probably represents yet another distinct species. We are still left with the question of whether subdividing D. ocoee or combining it with other taxa would produce taxonomic entities conforming to any species concept invoking genetic cohesion among local populations.

23525: Rana areolata and the sibling R. capito may be declining in parts of their ranges. Demographic (snout-vent length [SVL] and skeletochronologically estimated age) and reproductive (fecundity and ova size) characteristics were examined in a southern Illinois R. areolata population. Fifty-nine frogs (36M:23F) were sampled in 1996. Hematoxylinophilic lines of arrested growth (LAG) were detected in all cross-sectioned phalanges. Male age averaged 3.53 yr (range = 2-5 yr) while female averaged 3.83 yr (range = 3-5 yr). Male SVL averaged 82.78 mm (range = 71-90 mm). Females averaged 89.61 mm (range = 79-102 mm). Age and SVL were positively related in males (r = 0.81) and females (r = 0.76). Male and female age distributions did not differ significantly, though male SVL distribution was smaller than that of females. Ova from fifteen clutches were counted. Mean clutch size was 4868 (range = 3208-6807). Female SVL and age were both positively related to clutch size (r = 0.87 and 0.64, respectively). Mean ovum/embryo diameter calculated for all yolked ovarian complements, and two oviposited clutches (at the blastula stage or earlier), was 2.05 mm (range = 1.80-2.20 mm). Ovum size and clutch size were negatively related (r = -0.68).

23526: Among tetrapods, scleral ossicles form a ring of small bony plates in the eyes of Sphenodon, lizards, turtles, and birds. The number of ossicles and their pattern of overlap have been used as taxonomic characters for lizards and birds; however, the ossicles of turtles have been considered too variable to be phylogenetically informative. We undertook a more comprehensive survey to assess levels of variability in scleral ossicles and their potential utility as taxonomic characters among chelonians. Ossicles in 432 eyes from 73 species representing nine out of 10 cryptodiran families were cleared and stained. The ossicles were counted and the pattern of ossicle overlap in the ring for each eye recorded. Bilateral symmetry, and extent of intraspecific and interspecific variation were analyzed. Number of ossicles ranged from 7 to 14 per eye. The most common numbers of ossicles were 10 (39%) and 11 (35%). There was a high degree of bilateral symmetry in the number of ossicles present. Within a species, the extent of bilateral symmetry in overlap patterns ranged from 39% to 100%. For the most common numbers of ossicles, overlap patterns were predominated by one or two very common patterns. Although number of ossicles alone may be useful in distinguishing some closely related species, it has limited use at higher taxonomic levels. The overlap patterns are very conservative and therefore of limited phylogenetic utility.

23527: We measured effects of three chemicals and UV radiation on Rana utricularia and Hyla chrysoscelis tadpoles using a center point- and chemical-free control-enhanced 2^4 factorial design. Rana tadpoles were introduced to 72, 500-l mesocosms (90 each) on 25 April 1997. UV radiation was transmitted or blocked using OP-4 or OP-3 filters (installed 16 May). Methyl mercury, chlorpyrifos, and atrazine were applied at 0, 10, 50, and 100 % of 0.4 mg/kg, 30 ppb, and 192 ppb, respectively, on 8 June. 23536: Although many studies have ascribed potential benefits of increased water availability during incubation to neonatal survival in turtles, none have directly examined how differential water availability influences the migratory behavior of the hatchlings under field conditions. 23540: Internal transcribed spacers (ITS1 and ITS2) are DNA regions separating the multicopy, nuclear ribosomal RNA genes. 23541: Most fishes are faced with one of two options for gill ventilation: physically moving their gills through the medium ("ram" ventilation), or actively pumping the medium over their gills via "buccal pumping". 23552: For the last decade, interest in modeling chelonian growth has increased and provided a framework for better understanding of this life history trait. 23570: It is generally recognized that the evolution of sympatric fish ecotypes found in post glacial lakes is the result of processes driving ecological and phenotypic changes. This translated into significant but variable Fst estimates between ecotypes, ranging from 0.041 to 0.225. Similarly, dwarf and normal ecotypes were significantly different in morphological traits, the squared Mahalanobis distance (D) varying from 1.81 to 12.69. 23578: While reduction and loss of external limbs are hallmarks of amphisbaenian evolution, internal girdle and hindlimb remnants in some amphisbaenian taxa have been known for many years. 23583: The zygosphene-zygantrum articulations of snake vertebrae are hypothesized to restrict or eliminate vertebral torsion. I observed axial torsion during lateral undulation and feeding in Pituophis melanoleucus. 23584: Widespread use of agricultural chemicals makes it increasingly likely that non-target wildlife could be exposed to contamination. 23587: Remarkable morphological similarity among the cascade (waterfall) ranids of southeast Asia has made them a taxonomic bane for 160 years. 23588: Deserts are characterized by extreme environmental and resource variation; many desert reptiles have the ability to tolerate these stresses through behavioral and physiological mechanisms. 23589: This study contributes to the knowledge of Amazonian herpetology by evaluating the mensurable and meristic characters associated with ontogeny, sexual dimorphism, and geographic variation of the Amazonian tree frog Hyla geographica. 23590: Thamnophis sirtalis is a widely distributed, highly variable, snake which is common throughout much of its North American range. 23592: The identification of brook charr conservation units and processes responsible for their evolution are prerequisites to the conservation and management of the species in national parks. 23593: We reanalyzed the data of a recently published study of higher-level snake relationships, which was based on a UPGMA analysis of alleles at four "slowly-evolving" protein-coding loci. 23598: Amphibians have been widely used as model systems for studying the early embryonic development of vertebrates. 23601: Gulf toadfish, Opsanus beta, are poorly represented in ecological studies and their reproductive strategies relatively undefined. 23605: The form of the relationship between values for organismal traits (e.g. clutch size) and organism body size has been of interest to biologists for >150 years. Despite this long interest, there remains considerable controversy over the appropriate statistical model to use in each instance. Such high correlations are infrequent in life-history data sets. Presently, two alternatives for slope estimation appear to be gaining support: major axis regression, and reduced major axis regression. 23608: Extreme phenotypic plasticity of the lip was discovered in a population of Gambusia hispaniolae during a survey of fishes to Lake Enriquillo, southwestern Dominican Republic, Hispaniola Island. Las Azufradas, a pool of sulfurous water, is tributary to the main lake (Enriquillo). It is the only known habitat for a population of G. hispaniolae characterized by conspicuously enlarged and papillose lower lip that has not been observed in any other member of the genus (although it is superficially similar to the lip of Cyprinodon labiosus, a member of Cyprinodontidae and also to Poecilia sulphuraria, a member of Poeciliinae). In a sample of more than 200 specimens from Las Azufradas, the enlarged lip was present in 100% of individuals, but no specimen of G. hispaniolae from elsewhere exhibits the character. The hypothesis that the population comprises a new species was tested by morphometric analysis of individuals from Las Azufradas versus individuals from other populations in the island. Other than the modified lip, no morphological differences were found. Common garden experiments conducted to test for plasticity showed that the enlarged lip disappeared after short periods of time under laboratory conditions. At the end of the experiment, no differences in lip size or shape were detectable among samples from Las Azufradas and other localities. Feeding habits and effects of food type were also studied. We discuss the possible driving forces that produce the phenotype.

23609: Ethnoichthyology is the part of science that studies the relationships between people and fish, including folk knowledge. Fishermen usually have knowledge on fish biology and behavior, which is often useful to ichthyologists. We conducted an ethnoichthyological study with fishermen from the impounded portion of the Piracicaba River (Southeastern Brazil), interviewing 22 fishermen (17 men and 5 women) using questionnaires based on pictures of ten fish species. We showed the pictures at random, in the same order for all people interviewed. Fishermen showed a detailed knowledge about diet, predators, spatial and temporal distributions, reproduction and migratory patterns. Many information provided by fishermen fitted well with the biological observations from the scientific literature. Fishermen exhibit a great knowledge on diet, predators, migratory movements and habitat requirements of fishes. This could be due to the constant observation of these phenomenons by fishermen and due to the importance of this information to the fishery. Fishermen known more about common and commercially valuable fish species, and known less about rare species. The value and abundance of the fishes, the usefulness in the fishery, as well the frequent observation of the biological attributes of abundant species are important factors influencing the Piracicaba River fishermen knowledge about fish.

23610: African sandfrogs of the genus Tomopterna have previously been thought to consist of six species, one of which is a tetraploid. A fieldtrip to Namibia, Zimbabwe and Zambia provided material which shows that the widespread T. cryptotis consists of three species. The previously restricted tetraploid, T. tandyi, is now known to be present throughout much of Africa. We present a phylogeny of the diploid species, and show that tetraploid populations are accumulating genetic differences.

23611: Supernumerary, or B, chromosomes are morphologically distinct chromosomal elements that are found in addition to the normal chromosome complement. They may show numerical variation within and between individuals and are highly variable in their effect, morphology, and inheritance pattern. These chromosomes, thought to arise either from the autosomal chromosome set or through interspecific hybridization, appear to evolve independently of the normal chromosome set. Supernumerary chromosomes are present in the Pacific giant salamander, Dicamptodon tenebrosus. Individuals of this species that we examined possessed up to 8 supernumeraries, with population means ranging from 0.5 to 2.67 per individual. Supernumerary chromosomes from two D. tenebrosus individuals were microdissected, cloned and partially sequenced to analyze their genetic make-up. We used these DNA segments as probes for use in Southern blots to determine whether or not homologies exist between supernumerary chromosomes and the normal chromosome set. The DNA composition of these supernumerary chromosomes and their origin and evolution in D. tenebrosus will be discussed.

23612: The mobilities of six protein loci were investigated in ten populations of salamanders (Genus: Desmognathus) in Northeastern Pennsylvania near the edge of the Pleistocene glacial boundary. Heterozygotes were found for three of the six loci investigated in six of the ten localities sampled. Based on comparisons with similar studies heterozygosity is attributed to influence from genetically diverse southern populations, rather than interspecific gene exchange.

23613: The H. viridiflavus complex is considered to comprise a number of sub-species, based on dorsal colouration patterns. The reliance on morphological characters for taxonomic purposes has resulted in some taxonomic confusion regarding this complex, with some researchers recognizing few, and others many subspecies. The aim of the present study is to use molecular techniques to resolve this problem. Frogs were collected from various localities throughout Africa and their DNA extracted and subsequently sequenced (12S and 16S rRNA mitochondrial gene). Results indicate that H. viridiflavus consists of two clades, each of which is a sister group to a different grouping of other species of Hyperolius. The more basal clade are from inland central Africa (Zambia, Zimbabwe), and the advanced clade from coastal South Africa, and east Africa (e.g. Tanzania, Kenya).

23614: The Neotropical genus Hemiphractus comprises 5 species. Frogs in this genus have long been assumed to represent a natural group of species. Their bizarre appearance, with horn-like, fleshy protrusions from their upper eyelids, massive skulls, and serrated lower jaw bones, clearly distinguishes this group from any other Neotropical frogs. Previous work by us corroborated the monophyly of Hemiphractus and placed it within the genus Gastrotheca — i.e., Gastrotheca is paraphyletic with respect to Hemiphractus. Herein we present some recent work on the phylogeny of Hemiphractus based on data from osteology, external morphology, and behavior. Parsimony analysis of 48 characters generated a single tree that fully resolves relationships among these species. This tree is highly congruent with Trueb's (1974) hypothesis of relationships among these species and allows us to discuss aspects of their biogeography and behavior.

23615: In pond-breeding amphibian species, dispersal between demes reduces the chance for local extinction. I aim to show that the level of dispersal is determined not only by the distance of ponds, but also by the quality of the terrestrial habitat between them. Toads (Bufo bufo) and newts (Triturus cristatus) in the United Kingdom and France were surveyed for their presence or absence in large numbers of ponds. Environmental data were obtained in the field and from topographical maps and satellite imagery. A stepwise logistic regression procedure was used to identify the ecological parameters associated with the presence/absence of both species. Dispersal scenarios were generated on the assumption that good habitat to live in is good habitat to disperse through. The several dispersal hypotheses are currently being tested against gene-flow estimates obtained from a variety of genetic markers (allozymes, mini- and micro-satellites).

23616: The phylogenetic relationships among tropical taxa are poorly known when compared to temperate counterparts. In frogs, this situation is compounded by a notoriously conserved morphology which yields few readily-apparent characters. Thus hypotheses of speciation and character evolution have often been constrained to limited data or relied upon gross similarity and contemporary biogeography. We have used DNA sequence data to investigate the phylogenetic affinities among the "30 chromosome group" of tree frogs of the genus Hyla. This group has representatives from Central America through the Andes, across the Amazon basin and into the Atlantic forests of Brasil. We compare the existing view of this group with the picture revealed by DNA sequence data.

23617: Six taxa of crested and marbled newts (subgenus Triturus) have largely parapatric distributions across Europe, with or without hybridization taking place between them. A combination of morphological, protein and mtDNA sequence data is applied to resolve the taxonomy of the group. In France, western Europe, hybridization between crested and marbled newts is unidirectional. This hybrid zone is spatially-temporally unstable and affected by environmental change, giving rise to a typical geographical pattern. Comparison of this zone with a cluster of hybrid zones in four taxa of crested newts in 'ex-Yugoslavia', eastern Europe, reveals remarkable similarities between them, suggesting that the same forces are operational across Europe in hybrid zone dynamics.

23618: The Banggai cardinalfish, Pterapogon kauderni Koumans 1933 has been the focus of the pet trade since its "rediscovery" a few years ago. Very little is known about the population status of this species which seems restricted to the sandy shallows of the Banggai Islands in the Indo-Pacific ocean. In an attempt to alleviate the collecting pressure on this species, a captive breeding program was successfully developed. The reproductive biology of P. kauderni differs from most Apogonids in several aspects. The spawn consists of a few large eggs, about 40 of 3 mm in diameter. Eggs are incubated by the male for approximately 19 days (25°C) until hatching occurs. The larvae hatch in a post-flexion stage measuring about 6 mm SL and remain in the male's oral cavity for another ten days. At the time of release, Banggais measure 8 mm SL, their large yolk sac is mainly consumed and they do not pass through a planktonic stage. Once released, alevines do not come back to seek refuge in the male's mouth and no association between male and newly released alevines persists. Juveniles take four months to reach 30 mm TL and they mature in another five to seven months. A summary of the ontogeny and larval development is presented.

23619: Moxostoma spawning acts involve one female and two or more males, and occur by intense quivering into gravel and/or cobble. In primitive, mass-spawning M. collapsum and M. anisurum, usually 3-5 nonterritorial males attend each act. Advanced species typically trio-spawn, a male on each side of the female. The most derived repertoire, in M. carinatum, involves two-male defense of spawning sites and, upon approach by a female, synchronized lengthy alignment (10-20 sec), undulation, and quivering (5-10 sec each). Nest-building and courtship are falsely ascribed to M. carinatum. Synapomorphies of anatomy, coloration, and behavior support recognizing the clade (Carolina redhorse (M. erythrurum) (M. robustum, M. carinatum)). In mass spawning, greater numbers of eggs may be fertilized and buried, but earlier-buried eggs may be unburied. In trio spawning the female is symmetrically held and pressed laterally to dorsolaterally during oviposition. In the more derived species, the two adjacent nest-holding (Dear Enemy) males repel intruders that perturb or dispel the female from spawning. It takes two males to tango, perhaps best so in suckers.

23620: Spatial abilities are important in mediating natural behaviors in snakes, such as localization of refuges. Eight snakes were trained to find the location of an escape hole in a circular arena, given a choice of eight holes. Learning was determined by significant decreases in the latency to find the goal and in the distance traveled to the goal. To date, most animals had not learned the task after 32 training sessions. Only two animals showed a significant change in behavior indicative of learning. These results differ from those obtained previously with corn snakes, Elaphe g. guttata, which can learn the same task within 16 training sessions. Manipulation of sensory cues after training indicates that subjects use different cues to find their goal. All animals were also tested for shelter preferences. Snakes were given a choice of three different shelter sites (submerged, on ground, elevated) over a four day period to determine the relevance of the arena escape task. To date, six animals preferred elevated shelters, and most animals show fidelity to shelters chosen on the first day. These results suggest that juvenile spotted pythons may be more motivated to seek elevated instead of submerged refuges.

23621: Declines in populations of some formerly common, widespread amphibians and reptiles in Idaho indicate the need for a statewide monitoring program. Such declines show that we can no longer assume that amphibian and reptile populations are doing well. The mark-recapture studies needed to document changes in numbers of animals are too expensive to conduct on a statewide basis. The best evidence that we have for amphibian population declines comes from documenting changes in the species occurrence over wide area. This suggests that an alternative approach is to periodically survey selected study areas for changes in the number of sites occupied by each species. Such a program could involve selecting 20 study areas around the state so that all species and ecoregions would be represented at least twice. Every year, 2-3 study areas (with 20-30 separate sites each) could be surveyed using standard techniques so that all would be sampled once per decade. If a considerable decrease in the number of occupied sites for a species is detected, further studies could be conducted to determine the extent and nature of the declines. We are testing this approach by repeating surveys conducted during the 1970's at two areas in southern Idaho.

23622: The South America characiforms called piranhas comprise nearly 60 described species, allocated to four genera, Pygopristis, Pristobrycon, Serrasalmus and Pygocentrus. Pygopristis is apparently monotypic, and Pygocentrus has been shown to include three species. Questions about the monophyly of Pristobrycon and Serrasalmus have been raised by several workers, and the general expectation is that Pristobrycon is paraphyletic. In this paper I examine the identities of nominal species of Serrasalmus and Pristobrycon, and discuss the phylogenetic relationships among those shown to be valid. Features analyzed include skeletal, morphological, soft anatomy, color pattern, squamation, and body shape.

23623: Juveniles of the black-water piranhas Serrasalmus manueli and Serrasalmus gouldingi are virtually identical in body shape, pigmentation and meristic features. In contrast, adults of these species are markedly different in body shape, pigmentation, and to a lesser extent in meristic features, and are easily identifiable. Our objectives in this study are to explore the use of some novel morphometric techniques in the analysis of body shape and ontogeny. One objective in particular is to determine whether small juveniles can be distinguished by body shape using relative warps analysis. The second objective is to compare the ontogenetic transformations in shape that produce the markedly different adult body forms from the indistinguishable juvenile body forms.

23624: Caecilians are circumtropically distributed amphibians exhibiting many adaptations to a fossorial existence including limblessness, reduced eyes and a strongly ossified skull. Perhaps none of their morphological oddities is as enigmatic as the presence of dermal scales, a character found in neither of the other lissamphibian orders. Most species of caecilian have circumferential rows of tiny scales in some or all of the annular grooves that ring the body. The size and shape of individual scales were once thought to be of systematic importance, though variation in these parameters within a single individual may encompasses the range of variation seen in the whole group. We used a clearing and staining technique to look at the pattern of scalation rather than the scales themselves. Data from fourteen Grandisonia larvata showed less than 10% variation in a suite of meristic characters. Data from single individuals of sixteen other species in all six families showed a wide range of variation from fully scaled to completely naked. Basal taxa such as Epicrionops and Ichthyophis are nearly completely covered, while some of the most derived taxa have no scales (Typhlonectes) or few scales (Geotrypetes). The pattern of scalation is sufficient to distinguish between genera, and, in some cases species. Data from several smaller individual G. larvata indicate that scalation begins in the posterior annular groves and proceeds anteriorly. There are two dorso-lateral centers of scalation in each annular groove from which scalation eventually grows around the body.

23625: The Avon Park Air Force Range (APAFR) is a diverse 106,000 acre federal property in south-central Florida. Many diverse wetland and upland habitats are embedded in a matrix of pine dominated communities. A major topographic feature of the property is a narrow central relict sand ridge (ie., Bombing Range Ridge). During a two year vertebrate study, we documented the distribution and abundance of a large percentage of the amphibians and reptiles observed on the property. Many records were observations made during road cruising activities. Additional monitoring techniques included dip netting, field searching and examining gopher tortoise burrows using a mobile camera. Of the 77 species potentially occurring on the property we documented the presence of 62 species. Based on known distributions and the habitats present on APAFR the absence of at least two species from this property is perplexing. Two xeric-upland endemics (Neoseps reynoldsi and Eumeces egregius) were not documented during this study despite intensive surveys whereas other fauna of this community (eg., Rhineura floridana, Sceloporus woodi, Tantilla relicta) were commonly encountered. Biogeography, not habitat degradation or loss, is the most likely explanation for the absence of these species.

23626: The island of Trinidad in the southern Caribbean Sea, supports one of the largest nesting aggregations of the leatherback turtle. While the presence of this colony is well known, the post nesting distribution of these females is not well understood. Studies into the dive behavior of female leatherbacks at this colony as well as in other colonies is well defined, however little is understood about diving and foraging behavior of the species outside of the nesting season. In this study, I use satellite telemetry to follow the post-nesting movements and diving behavior of leatherback sea turtles for one year. During that period the turtles swam in excess of 13,000 km and virtually circumnavigated the northern Atlantic Ocean. Dive behavior was variable depending on region and was likely related to food distribution. Maximum dive depths were in excess of 700 m. Detailed results of this study will be presented including a description of where the turtles went after leaving, their diving behavior as well as possible reasons for the routing chosen.

23627: A four year collecting effort in the Minacu-Uruacu region of Goias, Brazil, produced 36 species of amphibians (2 orders and 6 families), 6 species of amphisbaenians (1 family), 25 species of lizards (9 families), 56 species of snakes (8 families), 3 species of chelonians (3 families), and 2 species of crocodilians (1 family). 23628: Other than anecdotal information obtained from commercial turtle trappers, relatively little data relating to the alligator snapping turtle (Macroclemys temminckii) in Georgia are available. Further, the impact of the commercial trade of this species on Georgia populations is largely unknown. Two separate studies, one completed in 1990 and the other currently ongoing, were developed to enhance our knowledge of the present day distribution and relative abundance of the species in Georgia, as well as to develop appropriate plans for its conservation. Interviews with a commercial trapper extremely familiar with M. temminckii populations in Georgia, revealed that these turtles were trapped during the 1970s and early 1980s in all major coastal plain stream systems in Georgia. M. temminckii populations were found in all watersheds which emptied into the Gulf of Mexico. Commercial trapping efforts during that period resulted in the capture and sale of 6000 to 7000 adult turtles averaging 32 kg each from the Flint River system alone. 23629: Habitat segregation among related species has many ecological implications. However, the degree of spatial distribution differences in regions of sympatry is not well known for amphibians. Three-hundred sixteen ponds were monitored in three counties in northwest Indiana to determine if the spatial distributions of amphibian species differed. Data on relative abundance of the eleven most abundant amphibian species were tested by the Cramer-von Mises test, for differences between the way the populations of each species pair are distributed across the study area. Thirty-eight (69%) out of the 55 possible species pairs had significantly different spatial distributions. Distributions of all the species within families or genera were significantly different from each other, except among toads and leopard frogs which tended not to differ from most other species. The biological significance of the procedure in general and the results specifically will be discussed.

23630: Concerns over population declines and reports of malformations have led many agencies to become interested in inventory and monitoring of amphibians, especially frogs. Most of these programs rely primarily on calling surveys. Volunteers are often used in these efforts, and they are not necessarily trained herpetologists. For two years, my survey teams have conducted surveys of several species in a variety of habitats in western South Dakota. We have found that calling surveys are not necessarily the best census method for all anurans, and they may result in misleading conclusions. For federal lands in western South Dakota, we recommend calling surveys to monitor only one species, the chorus frog (Pseudacris triseriata). For most other species, calling surveys give misleading results or their success may depend on detailed knowledge of anuran life histories. Species which breed at temporary wetlands are easily overlooked when calling survey routes are designed. Calling behavior also appears to depend on certain climatic factors which have yet to be fully understood. Limited funds may be better spent on life history studies and on studies of chorusing behavior before calling surveys become favored as the primary method of inventory and monitoring of anurans across North America.

23631: Home range analyses are commonly used by herpetologists to test aspects of behaviour, demographics, reproductive strategies, and other aspects of ecology. Unfortunately, herpetologists (and other ecologists) often do not use the same rigorous standards when analyzing home ranges that they use for other statistical procedures. Home ranges are frequently estimated using different sample sizes, time intervals among observations, and total sampling periods, either among animals or among treatments. Using simulations and radiotelemetry data from snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina), I demonstrate that home range estimates are dependent upon these three aspects of the sampling regime. In order to adequately test for treatment effects, home ranges must be analyzed using similar sample sizes and time intervals. Ironically, one aspect of home range analysis which ecologists have attempted to improve is autocorrelation. Traditionally, autocorrelation is believed to violate the assumptions of home range estimates, and so ecologists often subsample observations to reduce autocorrelation. However, I demonstrate that the accuracy and precision of home range estimates may improve with increasing autocorrelation, and reducing autocorrelation may cause more problems than it solves.

23632: We studied a population of common musk turtles (Sternotherus odoratus) in Georgian Bay, Ontario. These turtles occupy the shallow shoreline waters of the many small islands in this region. Their habitat is fragmented because most of the area is land or deep water, which is unusable. Animals occupying fragmented habitat appear to have larger home ranges relative to those that do not because unused space between and around fragments are included in the analysis. Two home range estimators, minimum convex polygon and harmonic mean, tend to overestimate home range in fragmented habitat. Cluster analysis is an estimator which reduces the amount of unused area within the estimate. Using radio-location data from the musk turtles we compared the accuracy of these three home range estimators. Cluster analysis was only more accurate than the harmonic mean estimator. However, the variability in accuracy was considerably less for cluster analysis relative to minimum convex polygon. We concluded that cluster analysis is a more appropriate home range estimator for animals in fragmented habitat than the minimum convex polygon or harmonic mean estimators.

23633: Game theory has greatly improved our understanding of animal behaviour, and can be used to predict the outcomes of fights or contests between individuals. This theory predicts that an animal's role might be used as a cue for contest settlement, thus reducing the cost of contests. The objective of this study was to evaluate how role asymmetries in size and kinship affect the frequency of aggressive behaviours and the outcomes of male-male contests for food in hatchling snapping turtles (Chelydra serpentina). Snapping turtle hatchlings were randomly paired either with a clutch-mate (144 pairs) or with a non-relative (158 pairs) and were placed in an arena where they competed for 10 consecutive equal-sized food items. The number of times that each turtle acquired a food item as well as the frequency of two aggressive behaviours, biting and mounting, were recorded. The results indicate that absolute body size, body size ratio between competitors and relatedness of individuals are not important determinants in the outcomes of contests or the frequency of aggression. Clutch identity was a significant predictor of frequency of aggressive behaviours, but not contest outcomes.

23634: Theory predicts that in polygynous species males should disperse from natal sites more than females because dispersal will promote the ability of males to compete for mates. We tested this prediction in a polygynous population of collared lizards, Crotaphytus collaris, by determining the distance between the points of first and last capture for male and female hatchlings, and the distance between hatchling location and where males and females settled as yearlings. Distance between first and last sightings within the hatchling activity season was not different in males and females. A similar percentage of both sexes dispersed > 20m from the hatchling to the yearling season, and the average hatchling to yearling dispersal distance was not different in males and females. These data do not support the hypothesis of male-biased natal dispersal, even though our central Oklahoma population of collared lizards displays a strongly polygynous social system.

23636: Spotted turtles (Clemmys guttata) are listed as "Vulnerable" in Canada, and are similarly listed throughout the eastern U.S. Not much is known about hibernation in this species, therefore information on site fidelity and communal hibernaculum use may be important to the creation of conservation programs. We examined various aspects of hibernation in a population of northern temperate spotted turtles residing on an island in Georgian Bay, Ontario. Using temperature-sensitive radiotransmitters and miniature dataloggers, we monitored the phenology and temperatures at entrance into and exit from hibernation over 4 winters (1993-97). Nineteen hibernacula occupied by a total of 34 turtles were discovered; 12 hibernacula were apparently occupied by individual turtles and 7 were used communally (minimum of 2-6 individuals). Many individuals returned to the same hibernaculum in subsequent winters. Turtles entered hibernation in late September and October when body temperatures were approximately 12°C, and exited hibernacula in late April when turtles experienced temperatures of about 4°C. Turtles were protected from subzero temperatures in their thermally stable hibernacula (range 0.3 to 3.9°C), despite highly variable and low winter air temperatures (average minimum of -33°C). Turtles lost little weight over winter (loss of 2-4% of pre-hibernation mass).

23637: Populations of turtles were determined in three habitats of Pool 20, upper Mississippi River including an open river site, a slough, and a backwater. Baited turtle traps were used to collect turtles at each site between early June through September, 1997. Two hundred and eighty-three turtles in 7 species were collected during the study. 23640: During the course of field work over a 10-year period with the arboreal boa Corallus grenadensis on the West Indian island of Grenada, locals (e.g., farmers, forestry officials) invariably informed us that tree boas were not as common as they had been in the past. 23641: We investigated the role of underground refugia in the ecology of Heloderma suspectum, which spends over 95% of its time in shelters. 23642: The relationship between the spatial distribution of turtle nest sites and nest predation was investigated in a landscape encompassing a 12-ha freshwater wetland in west-central South Carolina. The goals of the study were to determine if nest predation is a function of nest density, and if two other spatial factors, habitat type and distance of nests from the wetland, influence survival rate. Gravid females of three turtle species (Kinosternon subrubrum, Pseudemys concinna floridana, and Trachemys scripta) inhabiting the wetland were monitored from the time they exited the wetland to nest until they returned from their nesting forays. Nests were monitored from the day of oviposition until they were deemed to have successfully produced hatchlings or depredation was documented. The three-year mean predation rate was 84.2% (80%, 88%, and 81% for 1992, 1993 and 1994, respectively). Modeling of the point pattern of nest locations suggests that nests were distributed at varying densities. Logistic and autologistic regressions provided no evidence indicating that nest survival is dependent on the survivorship of neighboring nests. In summary, no evidence was found that linked predation rate to any of the spatial characteristics of nest distribution that were examined. The lack of density-dependent nest predation is contrary to findings from some previous avian and chelonian studies, but supports the findings of other researchers.

23643: Mangrove communities are important habitats for fishes, yet significant extents of mangrove shorelines are being replaced by seawalls. Mangrove habitats harbored resident, nonschooling forage fishes (e.g., Eucinostomus gula) and larger predatory species (Centropomus undecimalis). Water depth and water temperature significantly influenced the abundance and community structure of fishes between mangrove and seawall habitats and between sites within these habitats. 23644: Data and observations from recent studies of hard corals and algae indicate that lagoonal patch reefs have undergone a major change in their ecology associated with the 99% loss in the cover of branching corals (Acropora cervicornis and A. palmata), a 75% reduction in hard coral, and a 315% increase in erect brown algae (Lobophora, Dictyota, Turbinaria and Sargassum). 23646: The distribution and abundance of fish species collected during the periods previous to the damming (1980), after the formation of the reservoir of Itaipu (Parana, Brazil) (1983-1989) and after 15 years the closing of the dam (1997) were analyzed. 23647: Recent research has suggested that the dynamics of fish populations and assemblages within habitats can be affected by the spatial distribution (i.e., isolation) of these habitats within streams. In this study, we determined the extent to which pool isolation (determined by the distance between adjacent pools) influenced fish movement and assemblage dynamics in two Arkansas streams. We marked common species from 14 pools assigned to two treatment categories: pools isolated by long-riffles (> 40m) and those by short riffles (< 10m). Repeatedly snorkeling each pool for three days in 1995 and 1997, we discovered significant effects of isolation. Generally, fish moved frequently among habitats (10-50%); however, combined movement from short-riffle into adjacent pools was six-times higher (24%) than movement from long-riffle pools (4%). Further, fish in short-riffle pools moved up and downstream with equal frequency, whereas those in long-riffle pools moved three-times more often downstream. Consistent with these results, we also found that assemblages in long-riffle pools were more stable than those in short-riffle pools (overall percent similarity, 87 vs 72%). Collectively, these findings strongly indicate that the spatial distribution of habitats within streams can have significant effects on the characteristics of fish assemblages and the processes regulating populations within individual pools. Because land-use activities can alter habitat spacing, these findings have important implications for fish conservation in degraded streams.

23648: Etheostoma rubrum is endemic to the Bayou Pierre system of west-central Mississippi and juveniles and adults are virtually restricted to riffles underlain with coarse substrata. Streams in the Bayou Pierre system are experiencing rapid headward erosion, resulting in the creation of new riffles upstream and the loss of riffles due to sedimentation downstream. Viewed as a metapopulation comprising linearly arranged local populations, we hypothesized that downstream populations of E. rubrum (characterized by lower density) might be maintained by more dense upstream populations through larval drift or juvenile/adult movement. Upstream riffles would thus constitute source populations contributing individuals to downstream sinks. We tested two predictions of a source-sink hypothesis. First, based on a longitudinal array of drift nets set above and below riffle habitats, we documented that both protolarval and mesolarval stages of E. rubrum are common, although not abundant, components of the drift. Drifting larvae were taken both downstream and upstream of riffles. Although a potential mechanism exists for transport from source to sink populations, length-frequencies (and inferred age structure) did not differ between upstream and downstream populations. Thus, predictions of the source-sink hypothesis are not fully supported and local downstream populations may be self-sustaining.

23649: The traditional approach in developing recovery plans for endangered species has been to directly sample the imperiled species. Utilizing surrogate species, however, provides a direct estimate of the imperiled species' biology while minimizing the impacts of direct sampling. For example, the Vermilion darter, Etheostoma chermocki, occurs in 11.5 kilometers of Turkey Creek, Jefferson County, Alabama. Although relatively common throughout its range, urban development continues to deteriorate conditions within the watershed. The surrogate method permits construction of a habitat suitability model using the sister species. This model incorporates multivariate statistical methods which identifies variables (e.g., discharge, habitat type, dominant substrate type, water pH, conductivity, temperature, relative abundance) that will be entered into a GIS spatial database. This model will then be tested on the surrogate prior to its application on the target species. Thus it is possible to construct a species recovery plan within the context of the species requirements, and compare expected results against field observations obtained with minimal sampling.

23650: The Peel-Harvey Estuary, located in south-western Australia has become very eutrophic since the early 1970s. 23651: Biology of the greater redhorse was studied in the middle reaches of the Grand River, Ontario from 1995 to 1997. Videographic observations indicated that males usually remained on or near the spawning riffles and females were either attracted by the presence or conspicuous behaviour of males. Males produced rapid snout vibrations which usually preceded spawning activity. Post spawning movements and habitat use were determined using radio telemetry. After spawning, most fish moved several kilometres downstream and occupied deeper margins of riffles, usually in aggregation with conspecifics. By early summer, fish had dispersed evenly throughout the 17 km study reach. An access point creel survey indicated that there was a significant recreational fishery targeting greater redhorse, although anglers were unsure of the correct name for the species. 23652: Artificial reefs currently play only a minor role in fisheries or ecosystem management. The most notable example is their use in the spiny lobster fishery. Further examination of the role that artificial reefs can play in fisheries management needs to be explored. An example may be with regard to facilitating recruitment of juvenile and young adult serranid fishes (grouper and seabass) from inshore grassbeds to offshore, natural reefs. Further, artificial reefs can play a significant role in sanctuary and marine reserve programs. Moreover, purposeful and timed exploitation/rehabilitation of fish assemblages through artificial reefs may help sustain both fisheries and fish assemblages. Artificial reefs may not be effective in habitat mitigation where natural habitat has been destroyed. Information on the complete role that reefs play in trophic dynamics therefore needed. Additionally, an understanding of the time and spatial scales necessary to effect management objectives is essential. While, most artificial reef research, to date, has been directed toward fish and fish assemblages, additional insight into ecological processes and large scale ecosystem management may be gleaned through their study. In the future, artificial reefs construction and deployment design should be directed toward adding to our knowledge base to better manage nearshore and coastal ecosystems. Interagency, interstate, and international cooperation are the cornerstones for this endeavor. Both the positive and negative features of artificial reef deployment as a management tool need to be understood before they are generally accepted as a ecosystem management alternative.

23654: The notochord of the lamprey is a solid cylindrical organ consisting of a cellular medulla surrounded by an extracellular fibrous sheath and an elastic externa. The base of the medulla consists of a layer of columnar cells with an extensive network of rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria. The cytoplasm of these cells also contains distinct lipid droplets and a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. The vacuoles in the cells located in the middle of the medulla are reinforced with a peripheral network of intermediate filaments. These cells are interconnected with numerous desmosomes. Lipid droplets and huge deposits of glycogen granules are also observed in the vacuolated cells. The fibrous sheath is made of several layers of collagen fibers. Interspersed between the collagen layers are deposits of extracellular matrix similar to that found in the elastic externa. The elastic externa is an amorphous layer of extracellular matrix that appears to be secreted by the fibroblasts and chondroblasts that surround the periphery of the notochord. There are several differences in the organization of the lamprey notochord when compared to the fine structure of the sturgeon and lungfish notochord (J. Morphol. 1998). These differences may have functional and phylogenetic implications that remain to be determined.

23655: Remoras (Echeneididae: Carangoidei) are medium sized, specialized pelagic fishes, inhabiting the warm water of the world. Remoras are found in close association with certain marine animals and inanimate objects. In all cases remoras use their sucking disc to attach to smooth surfaces. An osteological examination of cleared and stained remoras reveals that the disc is homologous with the dorsal fin of other percoids. The disc is composed of 4 structures: proximal, medial and distal pterygiophores, and the dorsal spines. These 4 structures are serially repeated to form the disc. The dorsal spine is reduced in size and enclosed in the fin membrane. The paired distal pterygiophore forms the denticulated laminae, and also supports the spine. The medial pterygiophore forms the perimeter of the disc, and supports the laminae forming a hinged joint which allows rotation. The proximal pterygiophore supports the entire unit, it connects to both the laminae and the medial pterygiophore. Each of these units is connected to the previous one by the proximal pterygiophore. The remora attaches itself by pressing the disc against a surface and rotating the distal pterygiophore around the hinged joint. This increases the volume of the sealed chamber creating a partial vacuum.

23656: The postembryonic development of the cartilaginous cephalic skeleton in Solea solea (Linne) was observed from hatching to the juvenile stage. Fry were trypsin-cleared and alcian-blue stained. At hatching, S. solea displays no cartilaginous structure. On day 3, the fry exhibit trabecular bars, Meckel's cartilages, palatoquadrates, hyosymplectics, hyoid bars, the first two ceratobranchials and basibranchials 1-3. On day 4, ceratobranchials 3 and 4 form. On day 12, short taeniae marginales are formed on the well-developed otic capsules and the branchial basket is nearly complete. On day 14, cartilage reduction begins as the posterior part of the trabecula communis separates from the otic capsules. On day 18, metamorphosis begins. The tectum posterius completes posteriorly the braincase dome. On day 20, the left eye moves to the median crest of the head and the right eye shifts a bit downwards. Consequently, displacement of the right eye induces a deformation extending to the right pterygoid process. On day 23, both eyes are located on the same side. On day 29, cartilage reduction affects the hyosymplectics; it continues with the first two ceratobranchials on day 32 and with the otic capsules on day 40.

23657: Xenopoecilius oophorus is a member of the basal clade of Adrianichthyidae.
