23658: According to Lindsey (1975), pleomerism is a correlation among related animal species between their numbers of meristic parts and their characteristic body sizes. Lindsey found a striking tendency for vertebral number to be positively correlated with maximum length in many families of fish; however, he did not find the same correlation among 36 species of the family Gobiidae in his analysis. Data on the maximum recorded size, numbers of vertebrae, fin-rays (in dorsal, anal, and pectoral fins), and scales in longitudinal row were taken from published reviews of the gobiid species occurring in the Indo-West-Pacific (120 species), South African (107), North East Atlantic (73), Black Sea (26) regions. 23659: Fishes use their pectoral fins for a variety of locomotor functions including providing thrust for rectilinear movement. 23660: Comparative osteology of the nominal species Campostoma anomalum was investigated across most of its geographic range in North America. 23661: Sperm competition is one vehicle by which males compete with each other for reproductive success. This paper examines sperm competition between the specialized cuckolder and parental male life histories of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). First, we find that the investment in total sperm production is higher in cuckolders than parentals and within cuckolders, males that have higher sperm production obtain higher fertilization success. The alternative male reproductive life histories of bluegill therefore utilize sperm in different ways to compete for reproductive success. Cuckolders invest in quantity because they always face sperm competition, while parentals invest in quality because they only rarely face sperm competition. 23662: Sturgeons (Osteichthyes: Acipenseridae) are evolutionary relicts with a wide distribution in the northern hemisphere. The historical biogeography of their association with their diverse assemblage of host specific parasites is explored using phylogenetic systematics and information from geology, paleontology and paleogeography. The patterns indicate historical exchanges with a variety of host taxa and low levels of conspeciation, resulting in small clades of widely distributed parasite species. Sister taxa of parasites generally exhibit allopatric patterns associated with discrete landmasses and basins. A trans-Atlantic track involving Acipenser oxyrhynchus and A. sturio and a trans-Pacific track involving A. medirostris are evident. The parasite relationships also support a historical connection between North America and North Asian freshwater sturgeons (A. fulvescens and A. baeri or their ancestors) and the biogeographical and phylogenetic relationship of A. fulvescens and A. brevirostrum. Based on these parascript studies, it is hypothesized that a former contiguous distribution of Palaeartic and Neartic sturgeons was fragmented by climatic and tectonic events in the Tertiary causing displacement of the lake sturgeon lineage and its association with the Gulf of Mexico drainages.

23663: Surgeonfishes harbor a group of gut symbionts that include the largest known Eubacteria (cell lengths of 30 um to >500 um). Because the bacteria are acquired after larval surgeonfishes settle from the plankton, the fish/symbiont system in the Hawaiian Archipelago and other north Pacific locations provides an opportunity to address questions about evolution of host and symbionts within and among hosts, within and among islands, and among island systems. We have surveyed microbes in host surgeonfishes from Hawaii, Maui, Oahu, Kauai, French Frigate Shoals, Pearl & Hermes, and Midway Islands in the Hawaiian Archipelago, as well as from the Red Sea, Great Barrier Reef, Tuvalu, Moorea (French Polynesia), Ishigaki Island (Japan) and Gulf of California. A variety of structural morphs of the bacteria, differing in maximum size, cell shape, and the number and mode of formation of daughter cells, have been recorded from all sites except the Gulf. Preliminary molecular studies suggest local divergence of microbes within a single host, at least for widely separated localities.

23664: Xenopoecilius oophorus is a member of the basal clade of Adrianichthyidae. 23665: Parasites may play an important role in fish life history and mating system evolution. This paper examines parasite loads in a natural colony of bluegill sunfish (Lepomis macrochirus). 23666: Lampetra aepyptera is a widespread species of non-parasitic lamprey found throughout the eastern United States. 23667: Reef fish assemblages are strongly influenced by reef structure. In areas where visibility is poor, specific visual census methods are necessary to determine the fish community structure. 23668: Two key resources are generally thought to limit salmonid populations in streams: the supply of food and the amount of suitable space within the channel. However, the relative influence of these limiting factors can change seasonally. Both food and habitat availability can affect individual fitness, but to what extent does each factor influence salmonid growth and survival on a seasonal basis? I performed a summer field experiment to directly test the effect of food and cover on growth and survival of stream-dwelling coastal cutthroat trout (Oncorhynchus clarki clarki). Using a 2x2 factorial design, I manipulated food and cover in stream enclosures containing individually marked trout. Fish receiving food addition experienced growth rates more than 25 times higher than those of unfed fish. There was no effect of cover on either growth or survival. These results indicate that trout were severely food-limited during summer. During winter, I combined a mark-recapture study of fish with stream habitat surveys to determine the extent to which habitat complexity limits growth and survival. Finally, to address how summer growth affects over-winter survival, I monitored fish released back into the stream from the summer experiment throughout winter.

23671: Spatial and temporal patterns in trophic structure of fishes from Agua Nanci creek, upper Parana river basin (Brazil) were assessed. Three monthly samples were taken from May 1996 to January 1997 using electrofishing, in three segments of the creek (near the spring, middle of its extension, and near the mouth). 23673: Decline in frog and tadpole populations may alter trophic structures and ecosystems. The field component of this project involved two phases - experimental manipulations in enclosures and landscape-level comparison of unmanipulated ponds with and without tadpoles. 23674: Low-head dams are a possible means to control spawning migration of parasitic sea lamprey, Petromyzon marinus, in tributary streams of the Laurentian Great lakes. 23675: Little is known about the ecology of stream-dwelling coho salmon (Oncorhynchus kisutch) in the Lake Superior drainage. Unlike in their native range of the Pacific Northwest, Lake Superior coho salmon inhabit streams characterized by low winter flows and highly variable summer flows. In all habitats, coho occupied focal positions in the main channel; however, fish were more tightly distributed and closer to the streambanks in simple pools. Aggressive interactions also were more common in simple pools although dominance hierarchies were observed in the majority of all pools. These results are in sharp contrast with research findings from pacific streams, which generally show coho moving to protected habitats and becoming less aggressive with the onset of high flows in winter. This study provides new insights into the behavioral plasticity of coho salmon and should aid in efforts to manage Great Lake populations.

23676: We assessed how biotic and abiotic factors influence the local diversity (alpha diversity) of fish communities in two rainforest streams (Itingucu e Tetequera) in the southeastern Brazil. 23677: The assemblage of rainforest snakes of the Manaus region, Central Amazon, was studied from 1991 to 1995. Fieldwork resulted in nearly 800 snakes of 66 forest species. Nearly all inactive snakes were found on the vegetation. In relation to time of activity, 41% of 62 species seem to be strictly diurnal, 21% strictly nocturnal, and 38% both diurnal and nocturnal. The commonest prey were lizards (consumed by 58% of the species), frogs (39%), mammals (23%), birds (18%), and snakes (16%). 23678: The genus Bothrops is composed by at least five monophyletic clades. We present original data on the feeding habits of 12 species, encompassing all five clades. 23680: Seasonal variation in sex ratio is well documented for many species of turtles, and is largely attributable to a seasonal increase in temperature. If this trend were due to a minor systematic shift in incubator temperature, the lower proportions of males should have been associated with a decrease in incubation time (laying to hatching) as both incubation time and proportion of males decrease with increasing temperature. 23683: Herbivory is a derived feeding characteristic that has evolved independently several times in all the major phyla and classes of metazoans. Bony fishes are no exceptions to this. 23684: Spatial and temporal patterns in the distribution, composition and fish assemblage structure and their relation to physical gradients were assessed. 23685: Both biomass and abundance data are commonly utilized in characterization of ecological system dynamics; however, questions exist as to which approach is best-suited for long-term studies. 23686: Central to the hierarchical theory is the concept that organisation results from differences in process rates. 23687: The evolution of viviparity in the genus Sceloporus is associated with a shift from the spring mating and late summer hatching observed for oviparous species to fall mating and spring birth observed for viviparous species. The scalaris group provides a model system to evaluate this transition, as the sister species S. aeneus and S. bicanthalis are oviparous and viviparous, respectively. We studied the reproductive cycles of two populations of S. aeneus and three of S. bicanthalis. The timing of the reproductive cycle of S. aeneus was as expected for an oviparous species. The timing of the reproductive cycle of S. bicanthalis, was, however, intermediate between oviparous and typical viviparous species. Like S. aeneus, hatchlings of S. bicanthalis are produced in late summer. More like typical viviparous species, however, mating by S. bicanthalis occurs in the winter. In the scalaris group, thus, the evolution of viviparity is associated with an earlier initiation of the breeding season (spring to previous winter), but the shift from fall to spring parition occurs after viviparity becomes stablished. The benefit of spring birth by viviparous species is that female hatchlings reach sexual maturity and breed by fall.

23688: A marked sexual dimorphism was observed in the height of the second dorsal fin in the Patagonian shore fish Patagonotothen sima. In order to explore whether other morphometric features would also contribute to sexual dimorphism in the species, a non-parametric multivariate analysis (Fisher's Linear Discriminant Function) was applied to a matrix of 16 body part measurements of 20 male and 20 female specimens (a random sample taken from of a total of 62 specimens) of P. sima obtained in Argentine Patagonian waters. 23689: The hatching success of bog turtle (Clemmys muhlenbergii) eggs from a single population was examined at a site in eastern Pennsylvania. Between 1993 and 1994 we compared naturally incubated hatching success with artificially incubated eggs. Bog turtles lay their eggs in various types of Carex grass tussocks within their marshy habitat. In 1993, 17 eggs in four clutches (four separate nest locations) were discovered. Seven eggs (two clutches) from two separate nests were left in the field to incubate naturally. Eggs were hatched in the laboratory at ambient cycling temperatures between 32.5 °C during the day and 19.0 °C at night (Mean 25.5 °C). Of the seven eggs, 3 hatched (42.8%) and 4 (57.2%) were removed by an unknown predator prior to hatching, whereas 90% of the 10 eggs incubated in the laboratory hatched successfully with only one infertile egg. In 1994, seven nests containing 10 clutches (33 eggs) were discovered. Twenty-one eggs at seven nests were left in the field and 12 were removed to the laboratory. All eggs removed from the field in 1994 were replaced with exact-size paraffin wax eggs. Ten (47.6%) of the real eggs left in the field were removed from the nests by a predator (possibly a small mammal), two (9.5%) were broken (presumably by another nesting female at the same site), and three (14.3%) failed to hatch. In addition, four of the wax eggs were removed by a predator. All of the eggs incubated in the laboratory hatched (100%). The results of this study suggests that predation on eggs by an unknown small mammal is a contributing source of mortality at this colony. Natural hatching success may also be reduced by infertility and poorly understood developmental problems.

23690: The evolution of viviparity in reptiles is presumably associated with a reduced clutch size and increased relative clutch mass. We tested this idea by comparing the clutch size and relative clutch mass of one population of S. aeneus and three populations of S. bicanthalis. Clutch size and reproductive effort varied among populations of S. bicanthalis, but not between S. aeneus and S. bicanthalis. Therefore, the evolution of viviparity has not been associated with shifts in reproductive allocation by S. bicanthalis. The only life history difference between these two species is that the viviparous S. bicanthalis reaches sexual maturity at a smaller size and sooner than the oviparous S. aeneus.

23691: The Indo-Pacific scorpaeniform family, Caracanthidae, contains a single genus of four or five known species. These fish are small-sized and live cryptically within highly branching corals. A histological examination of the gonads of nine specimens of C. maculatus, collected in Papua New Guinea, revealed an unusual and possibly unique gonad architecture. In females, the ovigerous tissue within each ovarian lobe is centrally located and surrounded almost entirely, except most anteriorly, by a peripheral lumen. Early-stage oocytes are located in the center of the germinal tissue; vitellogenic oocytes are situated on the periphery or extend into the lumen on a tissue pedicel. In spermiated testes of males, the spermatogenic tissue is also centrally located and surrounded peripherally by a lumen but the lumen appears afunctional, since spermatozoa are only found in sperm sinuses located in the testis wall. In addition, the testis contains numerous early-stage oocytes. These latter features suggest that C. maculatus is hermaphroditic. Currently, I am examining a congener, C. typicus for the possibility of similar gonad structure and the capacity to shift sexual function; and also closely related scorpaeniforms, including velvetfishes, for the possibility of similar unusual gonadal structure.

23692: We will briefly review the development of the radio-acoustic positioning system (RAP) and describe the simultaneously tracking of five white sharks by the RAP over a three-week period during Oct.-Nov. 1988. The RAP determined the positions of these sharks tagged with beacons based on the arrival times of acoustic pulses at a triangular array of three sonobuoys. These were linked via radio to a field station in view of the buoys on Ano Nuevo Island, where tracks of the five sharks were displayed in real-time on a computer monitor. We will show computer-animated examples of movement patterns as well as graphical analyses of the spatial and temporal inter-relationships between sharks. The sharks spent a mean XX% of their time within the range of the buoys located near the island, remaining there both during day and night. Trajectories suggesting active pursuit of prey occurred at both times along a corridor leading from the island. Similarities in when three sharks tagged on the same day visited the island versus two others tagged on subsequent days indicated that the former had some social affiliation. When at the colony, the sharks usually moved independently of each other, except when attracted to a kill evident from a cluster of short and non-directional movements. Individuals at times spent much of the day in a small area, possibly lying on the bottom resting or waiting to ambush prey. During fall 1988, sharks will be tagged with transmitters that record their swimming depths and stomach temperatures in order to unequivocally determine when they feed (based upon stomach warming by endothermic prey) and describe the sequence of events associated with prey capture.

23693: The tools for remote monitoring of marine animal behaviour have grown significantly in the last few years. 23694: One of the greatest challenges to shark researchers is determining migration and long-range movements of sharks. While reports of seasonal presence of the Whale Shark, Rhincodon typus in coastal waters are common, no information has been available on where those sharks dwell during the "off season". Further no information is available on whale shark activities or environmental preferences outside of the time when they are observed near shore. Working with commercial satellite transmitter manufacturers we developed a number of specialized transmitters for whale sharks. Between 1993 and 1996 ~17 of these PTTs (of 3 different types) were deployed and monitored. Results of this research, including the successful tracking of one shark for 13 months will be described. Data as to preferred depths and water temperatures were also relayed by some of the transmitters and will be presented. 23695: The investigation of calling energetics in frogs provides an opportunity to integrate studies of behavioral performance with whole animal physiology, muscle structure, and muscle biochemistry. Measurements of oxygen consumption by calling males have shown that metabolic rates increase by up to 25 times resting rate. Structural features of the trunk muscles that provide the power for call production, including mitochondrial density, capillary density, and abundance of lipid reserves, are all positively correlated with calling rate. Activities of enzymes that are important in aerobic metabolism and fatty acid metabolism are much higher in species with high calling rates than in those with low calling rates. Pairwise comparisons of closely-related species show the same pattern: those with high calling rates have muscles that can sustain higher levels of call production than do those with low calling rates. Patterns of energy substrate use reflect patterns of call production. Species with high calling rates depend more heavily on stored lipids for call production than do species with low calling rates, and species with short breeding seasons deplete their energy reserves more rapidly than do those with prolonged breeding seasons and long chorus tenure.

23696: Advertisement calls of anurans usually have one or two emphasized frequency bands, which match fairly well with the maximum frequency sensitivity of one or the other, or both, of the two auditory organs, the basilar and amphibian papillae. At a finer scale of analysis, however, mismatches often occur between their mean frequency of conspecific calls in a species or population and the maximum frequency sensitivity of the auditory system. Such discrepancies could be a mechanistic basis for sexual selection, but the question arises: How well do the usual threshold measures of frequency sensitivity reflect frequency selectivity at the much higher signal levels at which anurans normally communicate? Although threshold measures and frequency preferences estimated from the same individuals correlate poorly with respect to small, but behaviorally effective, differences within a single frequency band, such estimates do predict reliably which of the two frequency bands is preferred by females in species that have calls with bimodal spectra. In some of these, thresholds determined centrally and preferences correlate well with estimates of frequency sensitivity at the peripheral level, but this is not true of other species. Examples from behavioral and neurophysiological studies of several species of treefrogs will be discussed.

23697: Male Pacific treefrogs, Hyla regilla, use advertisement and encounter calls to regulate inter-male spacing within breeding choruses. Encounter calls are produced when the advertisement calls of a neighbor exceed a threshold amplitude. These aggressive thresholds are plastic; i.e. males resume advertisement calling (accommodate) to repeated presentation of advertisement calls at amplitudes 4 dB above their aggressive threshold. Correspondingly, a male's aggressive threshold for the advertisement call is positively correlated with the maximum amplitude of advertisement calls of neighbors, measured at the focal male's position. The aggressive thresholds of males for the encounter call also are plastic but are not significantly correlated with the maximum call amplitude of their neighbors. This disjunction stems from the fact that males in stable choruses are not exposed to supra-threshold encounter calls. Accommodation to one call type fails to significantly alter a male's aggressive threshold to the other call type. Plasticity of aggressive thresholds, like plasticity of aggressive signalling, appears to be important in balancing the costs and benefits of aggressive behavior. The capacity of males to selectively accommodate to the advertisement or encounter call supports the hypothesis that these two call types are processed, in part, by discrete neural 'channels'. Because these two call types are highly similar spectrally, selective accommodation cannot result from sensory adaptation in the periphery. The two call types however, differ markedly in their temporal structure, particularly their pulse repetition rate. These observations support the notion that separate temporal filters exist in the central nervous system for processing these two call types. Recent neurophysiological studies have provided insight into the mechanisms that underlie this temporal pattern recognition and discrimination.

23698: Ectothermy is the norm among animals. It is known that aspects of both acoustic signal production and reception in ectotherms are temperature-dependent. Since female preference in some ectotherms is also temperature-dependent, understanding the genesis of this dependence in detail becomes crucial. The inner ear of anurans is unique in that it contains three organs which are specialized for sound reception. The amphibian papilla (AP), the basilar papilla (BP) and the saccule (S) are anatomically distinct, spatially-separate organs each with its own complement of sensory hair cells and overlying tectorial structure. The BP and portions of the AP respond exclusively to airborne sounds whereas other portions of the AP and the S exhibit sensitivity both to airborne sounds and to substrate-borne vibrations. Measurements from the auditory periphery of Rana pipiens pipiens suggest that in contrast to BP fibers, AP fiber tuning is highly temperature-dependent. Moreover, hair cells from the rostral AP and S exhibit a clear temperature dependence in their intracellular current step response, unlike caudally-located AP and BP cells. Finally, spontaneous otoacoustic emissions, which presumably reflect hair cell motility, are highly temperature-dependent despite the fact that the upper portion of the emission frequency range (600-1600 Hz) corresponds to the domain of the BP. A model is presented that attempts to reconcile these disparate results.

23699: In this paper I present an integrative model that accounts for the relationship between intra- and interspecific variation in male advertisement call characteristics in frogs and intra- and interspecific differences in androgen and corticosteroid levels. As androgen levels increase to a breeding baseline, size and myosin heavy chain isoform composition of the call-producing muscles of the males change. These characteristics are related to vocalization as they determine (1) force of contraction and thus call intensity and (2) contraction velocities and thus pulse repetition rates. As the males call, energy is expended and depending on the length and intensity of the vocalizations, corticosteroids are released during the vigorous exercise. Additionally, the nightly calling has a feedback effect on the production of androgens so that vocalization itself increases androgen levels. Individual differences in nightly call effort are reflected in the variation of androgen and corticosteroid levels among calling males. Interspecific differences in call characteristics result in interspecific variation in corticosteroid levels as well.

23700: Molecular analysis of the eye opsin genes reveals high rates of nucleotide substitution and C to T transitions. Nevertheless part of them is still functional and in the cave fish larval rudimentary visual cells a limited number of opsin genes is even briefly transcribed. Only one opsin gene containing a deletion was found to be probably out of function. The gamma s- and alpha A crystallin genes are not active during cave fish lens development although they do not show mutative alterations. The genes being responsible for eye and melanophore reduction are in part non-allelic in the different cave populations. 23701: The phylogeny, biogeography, and evolution of troglobitic characters were investigated in the Amblyopsidae using DNA sequence data from the mitochondrial gene ND2. The ND2 phylogeny is incongruous with current amblyopsid taxonomy implying that the genera Amblyopsis and Typhlichthys are artificial taxa. The genus Amblyopsis appears polyphyletic: A. rosae is monophyletic but not sister to A. spelaea. Genetic divergence among A. rosae from four different watersheds is equivalent to or greater than the divergence among different species and genera in the family. Typhlichthys subterraneus is paraphyletic among four lineages, two of which are more closely related to Chologaster cornuta, Forbesichthys agassizi, and Amblyopsis spelaea than they are to the remaining two T. subterraneus lineages. Mapping morphological traits onto the ND2 phylogeny suggests that convergent evolution of troglobitic traits (e.g., reduction of eyes and pigmentation) was common in the Amblyopsidae. Brooks Parsimony Analysis (BPA) shows that the ND2 phylogeny corresponds closely to geological fragmentation of the East-Central North American Highlands, beginning as early as 8 mya. However, evidence of late Pleistocene dispersals was also apparent. 23702: Explorations last year revealed a second locality for Prietella lundbergi, or a closely related form, in an isolated, 50 m deep sump about 50 km north of the type locality in southernmost Tamaulipas. Four specimens from here bring the total number of specimens of this taxon to 5. Water quality and the aquatic invertebrate community of this sump clearly indicate lack of connections to a large spring that surfaces nearby. The sump is apparently perched alongside large flows that discharge at the nearby spring. Blind populations of Astyanax mexicanus are known from nearby caves, but none were found in this sump, nor in the type locality of P. lundbergi. Repeated attempts using cave divers to obtain additional specimens from the type locality have failed. It is hypothesized that the single specimen known from the type locality had been displaced by flooding from a normally isolated habitat, similar to the new locality. Mitochondrial DNA sequence data indicate that P. lundbergi is distantly related to P. phreatophila, now known from at least 6 localities in central and northern Coahuila, but support monophyly of the genus. 23703: Males and females in Poecilia mexicana form mixed shoals in small rivers and ponds establishing a body lenght dependend hiearchy. 23704: A population of P. mexicana successfully colonized a lime stone cave in Tabasco, Mexico. Despite of the complete darkness in the cave, the cave living fishes have almost normal developed eyes. 23705: To enumerate and identify the genes involved in cave fish evolution, we are mapping the genome of Astyanax mexicanus. The BC progeny exhibited phenotypic variation in eyeball diameter, pigmentation (number of melanophores and presence of melanin), and relative condition factor (RCF or length corrected weight). Anonymous DNA markers were generated by AP-PCR (RAPD) and used to create a genomic linkage map (MapMaker). Factors for trait variation were placed on the framework map using MapMaker QTL. So far, we have identified 63 markers which coalesce into eighteen linkage groups. (The haploid number is 25 in this species.) On this map, we have placed three quantitative trait loci (QTL) for RCF, and one each for eye size and melanophore number, in addition to the locus for albinism. 23706: The Micrurus frontalis complex is an assemblage of poorly defined taxa ranging from the Cerrado regions of Central Brazil, through eastern Bolivia and the temperate areas of southeastern Brazil, to the Pampean regions of south Brazil, Uruguay, Paraguay, and Argentina. 23707: The western hognose snake (Heterodon nasicus) has been separated into three subspecies (H. n. nasicus, H. n. gloydi, and H. n. kennerlyi) based on various morphological features. 23708: Traditional studies of snake systematics emphasize univariate variation in some characters, and often ignore multivariate differentiation. I utilized discriminant function analysis to examine multivariate morphometric differentiation in head shape among four putative subspecies of Ninia sebae, a small semi-fossorial colubrid snake found at intermediate elevations in Central America. Linear discriminant function analysis can be used only if covariance matrices are the same amongst groups. If this assumption is not met, then quadratic discriminant function analysis can be used, however, this test is less powerful. Techniques which compare the structure of covariance matrices can be used to construct matrices constrained by commonality of matrix components, which may then be used in linear discriminant function analysis to more powerfully test a hypothesis. Using these methods, I found that the described subspecies of Ninia sebae are not well differentiated. The species appears to consist of two distinctive subspecies, with one wide-ranging group spread throughout southern Mexico southwards to Costa Rica, and another narrowly confined to the Pacific versant of southern Mexico and Guatemala, isolated by the Guatemalan highlands. These races can be distinguished using multivariate analyses, differences in dorsal coloration, and some univariate measures. Further studies may show them to be specifically distinct.

23709: The ridge-nosed rattlesnake (Crotalus willardi) is a small montane pitviper endemic to woodlands and forests of the Sierra Madre Occidental. Five subspecies of C. willardi are currently recognized; the two northernmost subspecies are restricted to patches of suitable habitat in the Madrean Archipelago or 'sky islands' of southern New Mexico and Arizona. Due to limited distributions and strict habitat requirements, the two subspecies within the U.S. are recognized as threatened or endangered either at the federal or state level. Crotalus willardi offers a special opportunity to investigate the biogeography of populations inhabiting the Madrean archipelago. Previous work using allozyme analyses and morphological differentiation suggested two possible hypotheses for the evolution and radiation of C. willardi populations: a shallow history model, implying that the northernmost populations result from a recent evolutionary divergence, and a deep history model suggesting that the first divergences were between the northernmost subspecies and all others. We used mtDNA characters to explore relationships among populations of C. willardi and reconstruct a phylogenetic tree for this species. Our phylogeny implies a combination of deep and shallow histories for the differentiation of sky-island reptiles, and raises questions about current conservation measures and their implication for the prioritization of intraspecific variation in this species.

23710: The pattern of geographical variation in morphology of the endemic skink Chalcides sexlineatus is highly correlated to ecological variation within the small (1532 km²) oceanic island of Gran Canaria. Sequencing of a fragment from the 12S rRNA region of the mtDNA indicated considerable within-island sequence divergence, and revealed the presence of three ancient lineages. Substantial geographical structuring of these lineages explains the morphological variation, thus refuting the prima facie case of differentiation in situ arising through climate-mediated variation in selection pressures as the cause. Very little introgression occurs between the principal Northern and South-Western mtDNA lineages, while introgression of mtDNA into 'foreign' nuclear backgrounds also appears to be limited. The time of divergence and spatial distribution of these lineages coincided with intense volcanic activity known to have occurred during the past 2.8 million years in the North of Gran Canaria, indicating that they reflect ancient population refugia which expanded to a secondary contact zone when conditions improved. Ancient within-island lineages are also found in the skink on the neighboring island of Tenerife (Ch. viridanus), the distribution of which are similarly related to the island's volcanic history.

23711: Characters from the mitochondrial genome have become the most commonly used source of data in phylogenetic analyses, despite arguments that these data are inappropriate and can result in misleading relationships. The results add to the mounting data that indicate systematic decisions based on mtDNA phylogenies should be considered with caution.

23712: Several data partitions, including nuclear and mitochondrial gene sequences, chromosomes, isozymes, and morphological characters, are used to test previously published hypotheses about the phylogenetic positions of basal clades of the lizard genus Sceloporus, and the relationships of Sceloporus to the former genus Sator. Our results confirm a recently published phylogeny (Wiens and Reeder, 1997) which groups Sator internal to Sceloporus, and both support a hypothesis of 'transgulfian vicariance' for the origin of the former genus Sator on islands in the Sea of Cortez. Support for internal nodes in our best tree is established through widely used indices (bootstrap proportions, decay values), but also through congruence among different data partitions, and the consistent recovery of these nodes by several tree-reconstruction methods based on different assumptions. Many nodes which are supported by a combination of several methods, including maximum and weighted parsimony, maximum likelihood, and minimum evolution models, are only weakly supported by the traditional indices, and this 'methodological concordance' is taken as strong evidence for their placement.

23713: Genetic diversity at 35 allozyme loci was examined in 9 populations of the taxa currently placed in Lacerta saxicola. Considerable population substructuring among the latter three taxa suggest that they may now occupy unique evolutionary tracks. 23714: Using mitochondrial DNA (12S & 16S rDNA and ND4) sequences, I investigated the biogeographical history and phylogenetic relationships of the snakes in the subfamily Crotalinae (Serpentes: Viperidae). I have included members from all proposed genera and, where possible, more than a single taxon to represent each genus. Phylogenetic analyses were conducted using both maximum parsimony (MP) and maximum likelihood (ML) as the optimality criteria. Monophyly of New World pitvipers is tested and determination of their sister group is presented. Biogeographical hypotheses as to the number of invasions into South America is explored and questions concerning the proposed paraphyly of the genera Crotalus and Bothrops are addressed. Taxonomic validity of certain Old World genera (Protobothrops and Ovophis) are determined, and their phylogenetic relationships are described.

23715: As currently recognized, the Yarrow's Spiny Lizard (Sceloporus jarrovii complex) exhibits amazing intraspecific variation in male dorsal coloration, such that the range of basic colors among populations is nearly as great as that among all reptiles (e.g., green, black, red, blue, yellow, gray, brown). In this study, we use phylogenetic methods to address two basic questions: (1) how much of the color variation is intraspecific versus interspecific? and (2) what is the evolutionary history of color variation in the S. jarrovii complex? Parsimony and maximum likelihood analyses of DNA sequence data (1.8 kb) from the mitochondrial 12S and ND4 genes for 17+ populations of Sceloporus jarrovii (including the type localities of all seven subspecies) and several related species, along with morphological data, suggest the following preliminary results: (1) Sceloporus jarrovii is polyphyletic within the torquatus species group and consists of at least four evolutionary species, (2) striking color variation exists both within and between the evolutionary species currently referred to S. jarrovii, (3) most of the conspicuous male color morphs seem to have evolved independently from relatively dull colored monochromatic ancestors, and the blue color morph has evolved twice.

23716: The salt marsh snake, Nerodia clarkii, is the only North American snake species restricted to brackish water habitats and has evolved unique physiological and behavioral specializations associated with a saline environment. Two of the three subspecies (N. c. compressicauda and N. c. taeniata) are endemic to Florida and are threatened by progressive destruction of coastal wetland habitat. By using the subspecies as the focal taxonomic division in conservation and management programs, we imply that the subspecies is an independent evolutionary lineage worth protecting. As such, the taxonomic status and evolutionary history of subspecies must be ascertained prior to implementing conservation or management programs. Markers used in delineating two of the three subspecies have been vague or highly variable and have failed to consistently differentiate individuals of known identity into their respective taxonomic group. Further, the divergence of the salt marsh snakes from an ancestral freshwater form near the end of the Pliocene has been theorized, but with varying models. We sequenced the mtDNA control region of individuals from the Nerodia clarkii subspecies, Nerodia fasciata subspecies, and several outgroup taxa in order to elucidate the relationship among the salt marsh snakes and to better understand the evolutionary history of the group.

23717: Five hundred seventy two Sceloporus occidentalis from two nearby populations in Los Angeles County, California were examined for helminths: 200 from the San Gabriel Mountains (montane ca. 1584 m elevation) and 372 from the Puente Hills, Whittier (lowland ca. 150 m elevation). 23718: One-hundred and ninety-four Canadian red-sided garter snakes were collected from the Interlake region north of Winnipeg, Manitoba, over a two year period, in the spring and fall seasons of 1996 and 1997. This snake is host to a lung inhabiting digenetic trematode of the family Plagiorchiidae. The infection is acquired by the comsumption of tadpoles and frogs. These intermediate hosts harbor the metacercarial cysts that may further develop into mature, egg producing adults, when consumed. It has been reported that the minimum time requirement for the appearance of an adult trematode in the lung is greater than eight weeks. All snakes examined for trematode infection were preserved, measured for length, and gender determined. The adult trematodes were counted and removed, with their locations being recorded. The data were used to evaluate the prevalence (percent rate of infection) and intensity (number of parasites per host). The prevalence of the trematode infection was higher in females (35%) than in males (15%). The mean intensity was also higher in females (10+2, range: 1-65) than in males (5+1, range: 1-13). No significant correlation between intensity and snout-vent length was found in either sex. However, there is evidence to suggest that prevalence increses with snout-vent length. A group of long term captive (> 12 weeks) snakes were compared to the sample of wild snakes. There were no significant differences in the mean intensities of the wild and long-term captive animals. However, the prevalence in the females increased from 35% to 53% and increased in males from 15% to 30%.

23720: Under a 12 hr light/12 hr dark photoperiod, juvenile walleye pollock displayed a diurnal schooling and activity pattern, characterized by cohesive shoaling during the day, with a cessation of shoaling and decreased swimming speeds at night. Juvenile walleye pollock were not characterized by a distinct light threshold for shoaling; shoals gradually dispersed as light levels decreased and gradually recoalesced as light levels increased. At light levels below 2.8x10⁻⁶ mEs⁻¹m⁻² juvenile walleye pollock were so dispersed as to no longer constitute a shoal. Exposure to simulated predation had differing effects upon fish behavior under light and dark conditions. Brief exposure to a model predator in the dark, caused fish to swim faster than fish which had been exposed in the light. Chronic exposure to a living predator produced similar results; fish tended to swim slower when a predator was present in the light, but faster when a predator was present in the dark. In the light, predation can result in cohesive shoals, but in the dark, increased activity may accelerate shoal dispersal, suggesting that perceived predation risk has opposite effects upon the spatial distribution of shoaling fish under light and dark conditions.

23721: Fishes of the subdivision Osteoglossomorpha ("bony tongues") posses a functional novelty the "tongue-bite apparatus," located between the mandibular jaw apparatus anteriorly and the pharyngeal jaw apparatus posteriorly. Previous work on this group described a distinct behavior known as "raking" associated with this novel feeding mechanism. Using high-speed video (250 fields s⁻¹) and stop-frame kinematic analysis, raking behavior for two prey types (earthworms and goldfish) was characterized in the clown knifefish (Chitala chitala). Kinematic data will be presented that reveals raking is a modulated behavior.
23722: The Atlantic rainforest ichthyofauna is rich in siluriforms, with many endemic species. Seventy percent of the species recorded in the Betari stream, Upper Ribeira Valley, Eastern Brazilian basin, are siluriforms belonging to the following families: Loricariidae (eight species), Pimelodidae (four species), Trichomycteridae (two species) and Callichthyidae (one species). Between June 1996 and February 1998, I studied spatial distribution, activity patterns, and feeding ecology of these fishes in a stream section one kilometer long. Diurnal and nocturnal transects were made at different sites using snorkelling. Half of the studied species are distributed in patches, which water current, depth and type of substrate influencing their distribution patterns. Except for Otocinclus gibbosus (Loricariidae) and Trichomycterus davisi (Trichomycteridae) all other siluriforms studied are nocturnal. The loricariids graze on algae covering rock, mostly diatoms, organic detritus and sediment. Corydoras barbatus (Callichthyidae) feeds on aquatic insects and algae. The pimelodids are generalists carnivores, with Rhamdia quelen preying on fish and crustaceans, and Rhamdioglanis frenatus preying on aquatic invertebrates, especially insects (Trichoptera). This study is a contribution to the knowledge on the poorly known ichthyofauna from the Atlantic rainforest.

23723: We investigated the applicability of five species of butterflyfish as biological indicators on the Great Astrolabe Reef, Fiji. Availability and patterns of resource use by the butterflyfish were investigated. Individuals of 3-13 pairs of each species were followed and feeding rates and foraging areas were recorded. For four of the five species of butterflyfish, acroporid corals constituted the dominant food in the diet. Chaetodon pelewensis and C. citrinellus were not obligate corallivores, feeding upon coralline algae and filamentous algae. The remaining species were obligate corallivores. Chaetodon trifascialis and C. baronessa showed a preference for acroporid corals and can be considered feeding specialists. Chaetodon trifasciatus is a feeding generalist, with no clear preference for any of a wide variety of corals in the diet. Among specialists and generalists diet overlap was high, but between specialists and generalists there was less diet overlap. In addition, foraging areas of the different species overlapped, in some cases almost 100%, suggesting that food resources are being shared.

23725: The threespine stickleback is an intermediate host of the cestode Schistocephalus solidus. Prior research has led to the hypothesis that selection has resulted in a delay of the deleterious effects of Schistocephalus on stickleback until after stickleback complete reproduction. 23726: Population ecology of Rhamdioglanis frenatus and Pimelodella transitoria from the Betari river, Upper Ribeira Valley, State of Sao Paulo, was studied by the mark-recapture method between Mar. 1987 and Feb. 1998. After eleven monthly collections, 171 specimens of R. frenatus and 104 of P. transitoria longer than 80 mm SL were marked by tattooing in a 2.000 m section of the river. Preliminary estimates indicate populations sizes of 300-500 individuals for R. frenatus and 800-2500 for P. transitoria, with populations densities varying between 0.01-0.02 and 0.04-0.12 individuals m-2 respectively. These catfishes are sedentary, being recaptured at the same site of previous collections at rates as high as 85% for R. frenatus and 95% for P. transitoria. Upstream and downstream movements were recorded, without clear tendencies. Individual growth rates for R. frenatus and P. transitoria were 0.2 cm month-1 and less than 0.1 cm month-1, respectively, but preliminary data indicate those rates may double in the rainy season. 23728: Fish assemblages in 14 individual pools within a 1-km reach of Brier Creek, Oklahoma, were censused by snorkeling on 17 dates from 1982 to 1997, with intervals between surveys ranging from 2 weeks to 11 years. 23729: Stream fish ecology offers conflicting hypotheses about environmental and landscape factors controlling local assemblage structure, at scales from local "microhabitat" to "global" or macroecological. Using a large, time-delimited data base, spanning a wide range of local settings in midwestern North America, we tested suites of physical or landscape factors as predictors of structure or emergent properties of local fish assemblages, at scales including: (1) "within reach" (aquatic); (2) local area (terrestrial); and (3) within basin, and (4) among named river basins. In June-July 1995, we sampled stream fishes at 65 sites spanning 1700 km across Iowa, Nebraska, Kansas, Missouri, Oklahoma and Texas. At each site all apparent microhabitats were sampled, and environmental or landscape variables were documented. "Global" factors (rainfall, meteorological) were obtained from standard references. Basin identity explained much variation in composition of local fish assemblages as reflected by scores of "sites" in a DCA based on abundance. In a PCA including all environmental/landscape variables, latitude (a surrogate for "basin identity") was related strongly to fish assemblage composition. On the other hand, emergent properties of assemblages (e.g., richness) were not influenced by basin or latitude. Subsequent PCAs, based separately on within-reach "aquatic" and local area "terrestrial" factors showed that landscape within the stream (depth, current, presence of gravel patches) influenced species richness more than extrinsic terrestrial factors.

23730: The dramatic biological, chemical, and physical changes in the low salinity habitats of estuaries are thought to limit the number of resident faunal taxa. Remane (1934) first described this phenomena, a species minimum occurring near oligohaline salinities (5-8 ppt), from invertebrate assemblages of large stable brackish lakes. It has since been proffered as a general feature of the estuarine gradient, though examples from the primary literature are rare. Two possible complications to the location of this pattern in estuarine fishes are: (1) the large number of seasonal migratory species who exhibit changing salinity preferences with ontogeny; and, (2) the failure to standardize species richness estimates to a measure of sample size (i.e., rarefaction). I applied rarefaction techniques to seine and trawl survey data to investigate whether this phenomena is evident in fish assemblages from three tributaries of the lower Chesapeake Bay. Results of the analysis indicate a minimum can occur, and is most evident in systems with a physically long salinity gradient. Beta diversity calculations confirmed the region of highest species turnover was displaced upstream from the minimum (near 0-2 ppt), and coincides with the most severe changes in ionic ratios. Hence, distance to source pools of marine and freshwater taxa appears to interact with salinity preferences to establish the minimum. Excursions from most favorable habitats by a highly mobile species appears spatially similar to recruitment survival in sessile invertebrates, and may explain the similarity in pattern between the two groups.

23731: Observation Point at the northwest end of Normanby Island (Milne Bay Province) is the home of a taxocene with four to five species of sand divers, Trichonotus, one of them the recently described T. halstead. In 1997 and 1998 we returned to study their early life history. Purported gill-chamber brooding was not confirmed by dissections of many specimens. The sympatric species live in distinct harem territories or swarms on a sandy slope where they mate soon after sunrise. T. setiger, mating over coarse sand, deposit many small eggs. Mature females (~ 8.7 cm TL) had ovaries with 150 to 200 oocytes. When mating is over, eggs were scooped up with sand from the mating site, rushed into the boat, and observed live under special microscopes. Deposited translucent eggs (0.6 mm) stick to the sand grains. The clear yolk contains one large yellowish oil globule. Development was observed at 25-26 C: after 30 min, four cells had formed. Ten hours later, heart beat and blood circulation could be seen. Hatching occurred 13-13.5 hours after spawning. The just hatched embryos (ca. 2.2 mm TL, >38 somites) were translucent with completely unpigmented eyes. Initially the embryos were mostly resting at the bottom, occasionally wriggling, later darting around and into the water column. When motionless, they slowly sank head first. At 18 h a white pigment was observed around the anus, later white pigment accumulated around the notochord towards the tip of the tail, and finally in the head region. When one day old (3 mm TL) the yolksac had decreased in size; initially, the oil globule was about 1/4 of the yolksac length, now it took 1/3 of yolk size. At age two days the embryos had reached a TL of 4.5 mm. The snout region had become more pointed but neither jaw movements nor gut contents were observed, i.e. exogenous feeding was not yet started. These findings will be discussed with respect to the distribution of the sand divers and a possible direct development without a planktonic larva, a rare thing in coral reef fishes.

23732: Food habits data collected on Northeast Fisheries Science Center groundfish surveys between Nova Scotia and Cape Fear from 1981-1990 were analyzed to categorize abundant species into feeding types (e.g., piscivorus, molluscivorus, etc.), and to examine changes in feeding types through ontogeny. 23733: Discussions of the influence of riparian vegetation on stream health focus on the width of such buffer zones. Policy decisions and environmental regulations similarly use riparian width as the metric of importance. We sampled fishes and stream habitats in 12 stream segments downstream from deforested riparian patches 0 - 5.6 km long, all downslope from densely forested watersheds. We found that the strongest predictors of fish abundance and occurrence were area and particularly length of the riparian patch; patch width was a relatively poor predictor of fish occurrence. Limited riparian clearing may cause minor disturbance to the fish assemblage, but streams in even a heavily forested watershed cannot tolerate disruption of the riparian zone of much more than 1 km in length. Riparian buffer length should be given stronger consideration in stream protection and restoration plans.

23734: The Spiny dogfish is the most abundant shark in B.C. waters with biomass estimated to be approximately 200,000 t. Frequenting all depths within coastal shelf and slope habitats, the dogfish is a significant predator within NE Pacific ecosystems impacting a wide variety of vertebrate and invertebrate taxonomic groups spanning several trophic levels. In this paper we summarize the feeding habits of the spiny dogfish in B.C. waters analyzing several data sets collected during the 1970's and 1980's, and comparing them to published literature. In particular, we examine the spatial and temporal variability in dogfish feeding habits and discuss the importance of recognizing bias when attempting to estimate consumption rates of dogfish prey.
23735: Measuring food consumption in elasmobranch fishes has proven to be a challenge, and has resulted in the use of a variety of methods. In recent years, bioenergetics models have increased in popularity and complexity. These models take into account energetic costs of living (metabolism, wastes, and growth) in order to estimate consumption requirements. Bioenergetics models have been used to estimate consumption rates for a number of different species including lemon, sandbar, greyreef, galapagos, tiger, bull, spiny dogfish, scalloped hammerhead sharks, and spiny butterfly ray. Like all models, output is reliant on the quality of input data, thus direct measurements of the costs of living and how costs vary with environmental variables and body size are needed. A complete model has been assembled for the lemon shark, which through laboratory and field research has shown good cross-validation. However, accuracy of some models may be questionable due to inclusion of data from other species or by using laboratory data alone. Recent advances in telemetry techniques and captive husbandry may offer new opportunities for estimating energetic parameters in both the field and laboratory. Bioenergetics models may also be useful in quantifying the ecological association of elasmobranchs on habitats and prey populations.
23736: Much of the communication behavior of anuran amphibians and other vertebrates takes place in the context of reproduction. Many aspects of communication are dependent on, influenced by, hormones associated with reproductive state. Less clearly appreciated is the fact that communication signals influence hormonal state in a variety of vertebrates. Communication and endocrine state should therefore be considered mutually interacting systems. We have used anuran amphibians as a model for investigating this interaction. Our results indicate that the frog auditory system (carrying information about vocal communication signals) connects with several areas of the basal forebrain. Some of these areas contain gonadotropin releasing hormone cells while others contain populations of catecholamine neurons. The latter populations are sensitive to circulating sex steroid hormones, and may be involved in some aspect of reproductive endocrinology or behavior. The strong connections between auditory and endocrine systems in frogs suggest that the reception of communication signals may influence gonadal state. Experiments exposing frogs to conspecific calls support this. Males exposed to conspecific calls showed larger testes and changes in testes histology compared to control animals. In frogs, therefore, vocal communication signals trigger changes in reproductive physiology as well as reproductive behavior.
23737: Male anurans of many species advertise for mates vocally in dense aggregations where they may also interact aggressively with competitors. Recently, sophisticated experimental techniques have been used to address questions about the proximate and ultimate bases of vocal behavior of these animals. For example, with interactive playback an analog or computer-based call synthesizer is made to respond to a calling male after user-specified time delays. I will discuss how I have used this methodology in work on call timing and aggressive behavior. Our understanding of the calling dynamics of chorus members has also benefited from the use of multi-channel equipment to monitor the vocal behavior of two or more males. By using such a system in my studies of Hyla microcephala in Panama, I have found that males respond primarily to their nearest neighbors in the chorus. These results agree with recent findings on acoustically signaling insects. The behavior of males minimizes signal overlap with individuals whose calls are most likely to seriously impair their ability to attract a female. I will also discuss data on vocal interactions among male H. versicolor obtained in an artificial pond where my colleagues and I have manipulated chorus density.

23738: Xenopus laevis is a nocturnal Pipid whose native habitat is the murky ponds of South Africa. Two vocal behaviors had been characterized: the advertisement call of sexually receptive males and the release call (ticking) of sexually unreceptive females. We have recently described an additional vocal signal, a fertility advertisement called rapping, given by females just prior to oviposition. Rapping is an acoustic aphrodisiac that stimulates male calling and phonotaxis. Field and laboratory observations suggest that calling is confined to only one or two males at any one time, even in densely populated ponds. We have recorded several male/male vocalizations (e.g. chirping and growling) that might serve to establish male vocal hierarchies at the onset of the breeding season. I will discuss the significance of these calls in reproductive interactions and the cellular and molecular mechanisms that contribute to the sexually differentiated vocal repertoire.
23739: Midwife toads are a primitive group of anurans with parental care and highly simplified vocal communication. Several populations of Alytes have been studied in continental Spain since 1987. The distributions of call characteristics overlapped between different population and species. The covariance between temperature and call duration varied between populations of different taxonomic groups. Large male reproductive advantage was found. Phonotaxis tests showed that calls with lower frequencies (emitted by larger males) were more attractive to females than calls with high frequencies. In syntopic populations of the two species there was no sign of character displacement in the male calls, but female preference was different than in allopatric situations. Males increase their calling rate when exposed to a nearby competitor. The response is different according to competitor's size and competitor's calling rate. Call alternation between males is non-random. Although call overlap affects negatively female preference, call alternation does not decrease call overlap. Many of the differences observed in acoustical competition can be related with the differences in mating season length between species, and with the differences in selective pressures that these two scenarios incorporate (male acoustical competition, and female choice based in both dynamic and static call characteristics).

23740: The asian green toads have been profitably employed as a model for the study of the evolution of vocalizations by comparing diploid, triploid and tetraploid green toads on the basis of morphometrical and acoustical parameters. Since in green toads advertisement calls produced by males play an important role in mate choice, particular attention is given to their differences. Diploid toads show significantly larger body size and proportionally larger head and shorter limbs than both tetraploids and triploids, whereas no evident morphometrical differences were observed between triploids and tetraploids. Diploid advertisement calls have spectral and temporal properties that significantly differ from those of both triploid and tetraploid advertisement calls. Diploids produce significantly longer calls with higher pulse-rates and lower frequencies than those of tetraploids. Although strong associations are found between some temporal and spectral call parameters and body size of the calling male, our analyses demonstrate that the observed differences in advertisement calls cannot be explained as the by-product of body size differentiation only. We address the question of the factors that could be responsible for these differences: whether they are a direct consequence of poliploidy or, whether they should be seen as the result of an evolutionary process of diversification.

23741: The diversity of sizes and shapes within and among groups of fishes is one of the principal features of their evolutionary history. To understand as much as possible about the history of size and shape evolution, two important components must be explored: phylogeny and environment. The evolution of size and shape have often been discussed in the context of developmental theories involving differential growth (allometry), differential timing (heterochrony), developmental integration, etc. The purpose of this presentation will be to examine ways in which developmental theories of size and shape diversity are tested on phylogenetic and environmental hypotheses. The data comprise ontogenetic series of landmarks from clades of characid (Bryconops) and atherinopsid (Atherinella) fishes, fit to a reference form, from which the relative warps and relative-warp scores are calculated. Phylogenetic and environmental components of form change among species within clades is analyzed from both partial least squares confirmatory factor analyses. The results show that in contrast to expectations derived from the literature, large amounts of the variance in form-change among species are explained by phylogenetic hypotheses of species relationships.

23742: Barbus paludinosus, a diploid, small African barb species is widely distributed from South Africa to the Horn of Africa. It was previously reported from the Ethiopian Rift Valley and the closely related species, B. humilis, was reported from Lake Tana. We found B. paludinosus in the upper reaches of the White Nile, Blue Nile, and Omo River drainages. This species normally has a strong serrated spine in the dorsal fin. At two localities in the upper reaches of the White Nile and Omo tributaries, populations are characterized by a greatly reduced dorsal spine. In the same drainages, barbs with the normal dorsal spine morphology occur about 20 km downstream. The borderline between forms with normal and reduced dorsal spine morphology apparently coincides with the upper limit of distribution of the hexaploid large barb species, the only potential predator in the naturally depauperated fish communities inhabiting the upper reaches of the both river drainages. The distance between locations where the form with reduced dorsal spine occurs is more than 200 km. These locations are separated by the drainage system of a large tributary of the Blue Nile, where only the normal form was found. The morphological description of the Ethiopian populations of B. paludinosus with and without dorsal spine is presented. In order to test hypothesis about independent reduction of the dorsal spine in barbs from the two distant locations the karyological and mtDNA comparisons were made.

23743: The upper Coosa River basin poses a particularly perplexing biogeographic problem; it harbors isolated populations of many species of fishes otherwise found below the Fall Line. Over 17 species exhibit this distributional pattern to some degree. The already recognized high degree of endemism in the drainage (Percina antesella, P. jenkinsi, Etheostoma etowahae, E. scotti, etc.) suggests the possibility of cryptic species in other, more 'widespread' taxa. We examined morphometric and meristic variation across the range of the frecklebelly madtom, Noturus munitus. The populations in the Etowah and Conasauga Rivers possess a unique suite of morphological characters, including differences in shape and pigmentation, when compared with populations from the Pearl, Cahaba, and Tombigbee Rivers. We are in the process of analyzing genetic variation within this species and other closely related members of Rabida to identify phylogenetic relationships within this complex. Conservation and biogeographic implications will be discussed.

23744: Patterns of morphological variation in a group of western North American cyprinid fishes (the 'Gila robusta' complex of the Gila River basin of Arizona and New Mexico) has long puzzled fish taxonomists. Three different forms, (G. robusta, G. intermedia, and G. nigra) are recognized, yet their basin-wide distributions are a disjunct mosaic. Several hypotheses have been offered to accommodate this aberrant pattern: ecotypy/ecophenotypy (i.e., individual or populational response to local conditions), hybridization/intergradation (i.e., gene flow between differentiated species or races); and vicariance (an historical explanation related to regional hydrographic evolution). To represent these hypotheses, 33 sample locations were scored within the basin with regard to stream size, stream elevation, stream barriers, and paleodrainage pattern (the latter accomplished by superimposing sites onto maps depicting drainage patterns during six different geologic epochs). Morphometric data, collected from 25 individuals at all 33 sites, were then contrasted against the 9 test matrices using two- and three-way Mantel tests. A vicariance model was the only hypothesis proficient in explaining extant diversity of fish phenotypes. Of those reconstructions used in this model, only the Pliocene epoch was significantly associated with extant distributions of phenotypes.

23745: Gynogenetic female Amazon mollies (Poecilia formosa) mate with sexual males (P. latipinna) for successful reproduction. Studies show that males distinguish between conspecific females and gynogens, and preferentially mate with the former. However, the existence of gynogens indicates mate discrimination is imperfect. The Red Queen Hypothesis has been applied to this system suggesting the evolution of mate recognition is a coevolutionary 'arms race'; the lack of genetic contribution by males to gynogenetic offspring imposes selection for male discrimination that favors sexual females. This, in turn, imposes selection on gynogens to evolve characters that override male discrimination. This assumes gynogenetic females have evolved since their origination. Amazons originated with a hybridization between P. mexicana and P. latipinna at least several thousand years ago. If a coevolutionary hypothesis is true, extant gynogens should differ from ancestral gynogens. In this study first generation sexual hybrids were used as an analog for the ancestral gynogens to test this hypothesis. The predictions are gynogens will have an enhanced ability to attract sexual males, males will prefer gynogens over hybrids, and females will differ in agonistic behavior. The results of this study do not support these predictions. This suggests application of such hypotheses to gynogenetic systems be preceded by studies documenting the presence of evolutionary change in the species of interest.

23746: The sandbasses of the genus Paralabrax are New World fishes from the Eastern Pacific and Western Atlantic. Because the sister group relationships of the Serranin genera related to Paralabrax were unknown, they were resolved first. Osteological characters of the cranium and pelvic girdle support the monophyly of Cratinus-Paralabrax-Centropristis. The nine species of Paralabrax share derived features of urohyal configuration, pterygiophore structure in dorsal and anal fins, and structure of lateral line scales. A cladistic analysis based on morphological and molecular (cytochrome b gene) data suggests an early separation of two groups. One is predominantly South American and includes 5 species: dewegeri from the Atlantic (Venezuela-Brazil), humeralis (Chile-Peru), callaensis (Ecuador), and albomaculatus (Galapagos). Interestingly, the species clathratus belongs to this group but is found in the Northeastern Pacific. The other group is composed of 4 Northern hemisphere species: loro (Central America-Baja California), auroguttatus, maculatofasciatus and nebulifer (which are predominantly found from Baja to Central California). A hypothesis of relationships is presented. The species of Paralabrax seem to have evolved recently, in the last 4-10 million years, in contrast with the species of Centropristis, which appear to be significantly older.

23747: Patterns of geographical variation in AP-PCR (RAPD) markers were compared between two species of Poeciliid fishes. Thirty-one populations of the variable platyfish Xiphophorus variatus and thirteen populations of the killifish Heterandria jonesi were studied. These species overlap in range in central-eastern Mexico, in freshwaters from the Rio Tamesi drainage, south to the Rio Nautla. Six primers revealed 266 scoreable bands in X. variatus and 189 in H. jonesi (163 and 124 informative characters, respectively). Parsimony analysis of the data was performed in X. variatus by heuristic search for the shortest cladograms. The data for H. jonesi are still being gathered, and a subset of only eight populations was analysed (exhaustive search). The results support three geographically disjunct clades in each species: a northern clade centered in the Tamesi drainage, a south-eastern clade in the lowlands of the Rios Cazones, Tecolutla, Solteros and Nautla, and a south-western clade, more upstream in these rivers. We hypothesize that the same geographical barriers have affected the variation in both species. Relevant geographic barriers are not obvious, however. We suggest that the south-eastern and south-western populations are divided by elevation, while the northern populations are separated from the southern populations by unsuitable habitat of slow-flowing waters. It is also worth noting that populations of X. evelynae are nested entirely within the geographic range of the south-west clade and are indistinguishable from them. This raises the question of whether it is a valid species or whether all of the fish in the south-west clade might really be X. evelynae, rather than X. variatus.

23748: The study aims at resolving the taxonomic jumble among the African species of the genus "Garra" and establish their present geographic distribution. Extensive field collections have been made from Ethiopian freshwater bodies where the diversity of the genus is believed to be relatively high. Available museum specimens have been investigated. Morphology and morphometries have been used to identify the species. According to preliminary results, twelve forms (species?) are recognized from Ethiopia, five of which are new. Four of the "forms" are found in six other African countries while the remaining eight are known only from Ethiopia. 'G. dembeensis' is the most abundant and widely distributed species found in 75% of the drainage basins of Ethiopia and in six other African countries. Seven other species of the genus are known to occur in ten other African countries. Generally, the genus has so far been reported from fifteen African countries. The range is from Ethiopia in the east to Guinea in the west and from Chad in the north to Tanzania in the south. The historical biogeography of the genus is controversial.

23749: Interest in fluctuating asymmetries, random deviations from perfect bilateral symmetry, has spread to studies of sexual selection because of the intriguing idea that females could use the degree of asymmetry of a male trait to assess the genetic quality of potential mates. The evidence that females prefer males with symmetrical sexual signals, however, has remained controversial. A problem that applies to most previous studies is that preference for trait size can be misinterpreted as preference for symmetry, even when overall trait size is held constant, if females assess trait size by the largest minimum on one side. If overall trait size is equal between males, the asymmetrical males will have the maximum and minimum trait size, and so preference to mate with symmetrical males could actually reflect a preference to avoid males with the minimum trait on one side. Xiphophorus cortezi females preferred males with symmetrical bar numbers when the minimum number of bars was held constant. The strength of female preference for the symmetrical males with fewer bars was negatively correlated with the strength of preference the same females had for bar number. These results clearly demonstrate that females preferred trait symmetry in addition to trait size.

23750: I tested for female preferences of male body size in zebrafish (Danio rerio). My experimental design allowed females to view a small and a large male in adjacent aquaria. Time that females spent near males was scored from 20 min replays of videos. The average standard length (SL) of large males was 28 mm and small males were 22 mm. The average difference between small and large male SL in individual experiments was 6.4 mm. Females spent significantly more time near large males (average = 647 s) than small males (average = 550 s; ind. t-test, P < 0.02). When female time near males was scored only if the males were adjacent to the female, females also spent significantly more time near large males (178 s) than near small males (117 s; ind. t-test, P < 0.05). My current experiments are to test for female preference of male yellow coloration by filtering out yellow light from experimental males, and to use DNA fingerprinting to identify paternity in competitive matings.

23751: Multiple-male mating by females and the resulting sperm competition are widespread in animals. Benefits accrued by males that inseminate many females include increased reproductive success. However, the reasons underlying multiple mating by females are ambiguous since a single insemination can fertilize all her ova and mating involves potential costs to both sexes. One such cost is an increased risk of predation. Recent studies have shown that animals can assess the local risk of predation and, in response to high risk, females may decrease their mate choosiness and males may increase their use of alternative mating tactics. If predation risk increases the relative frequency of sneaky copulations in males and reduces choosiness in females, then we predict a higher frequency of concurrent multiple paternity per brood in females originating from high-predation populations as compared to females from low-predation populations. To test this hypothesis, genetic data from a polymorphic microsatellite locus was employed to conservatively estimate multiple paternity in eight populations of the Trinidadian guppy (Poecilia reticulata) differing in fish predation regime. Our data suggest that, on average, the frequency of concurrent multiple paternity is three times greater in high-predation populations than in low-predation populations. These results further suggest that predation risk reduces the variance in male mating success and thus the opportunity for sexual selection within populations.

23752: Our observations of round goby nesting behaviour on shipwrecks in the western basin of Lake Erie using a video camera indicate that these fish spawn at much greater depths (7 m) than previously reported (< 2m). Of the species that approached the exposed nest (rock bass, smallmouth bass, yellow perch, logperch, round gobies), most behavioural interactions occurred between the guarding male and other round gobies. During 12 minutes of observation, there were 63 instances in which round gobies approached the nest and in 4 cases, intruders fed on eggs. In response, the guarding male approached (34 times), chased (18 times) and hit (4 times) round goby intruders. The response by the resident goby to the presence of rock bass (1 swam by and 7 approached) resulted in 6 approaches, 4 chases and 1 hit. The resident male responded to juvenile smallmouth bass (3 swam by and 1 approached) only once by approaching the intruder. The guarding male did not respond to either logperch or yellow perch. We anticipate that recruitment of round gobies will increase substantially in Lake Erie owing to the presence of artificial reefs (shipwrecks) and the ability of guarding males to defend nests effectively.

23753: Fundulus heteroclitus live in tidal creeks where predation risk varies with the structure of the microhabitat and time of year. Structure of the microhabitat varies as a function of the tides. Accurate recognition and response to predators is essential to the survival of prey. This study investigated alarm behavior of adult and juvenile estuarine fish, F. heteroclitus. Activity was determined in response to conspecific alarm chemical in relatively deep and shallow water (aquaria and fingerbowls). In deep water, in the fall, F. heteroclitus show container dependent alarm behavior. Both adult and juvenile fish showed a significant decrease in activity in response to alarm chemical compared addition of control. However, in shallow fingerbowls neither adults or juveniles show a decrease in activity. Adults also show seasonal context dependent alarm behavior. In winter adults in aquaria show no change in activity in response to alarm chemicals. Accurate responses to alarm chemicals may be those that are modulated by context, such as water depth, that reflects the actual risk of predation. Field experiments will determine if these results extend to the field.
