23754: Diet studies often measure selectivity, or the proportion of diet made up by specific prey types compared to their occurrence in the environment. This measure is the result of two events: the choice to attack that prey type and whether the attack results in a successful capture. This study quantified these two events separately in the juveniles of three species of sculpin (Cottidae) to compare their roles in determining the taxonomic composition of the diet. Choice showed a greater influence on the occurrence of harpacticoid copepods and gammarid amphipods in the diet than performance. Significant interspecific differences in choice of harpacticoids and gammarids were found to be correlated with differences in the occurrence of these prey types in the diets of the three species. Performance played a greater role in determining the occurrence of calanoid copepods in the diet than did choice. Species and individuals with high capture success on calanoids did not choose to attack this prey type more often than those with lower capture success. This study indicates that classic measures of selectivity will only reflect active choice or avoidance when capture success on a prey type is high.

23755: Diel behavior was studied on pairs of adults living in burrows and juveniles sharing these burrows. Juveniles retire into burrows at dusk and emerge at dawn to break into large swarms, feeding on plankton as far as 10 m from their home burrow at depths 4 to 34 m. Adults clean their burrows by spitting out sand and carrying out rubble. At night neither adults nor juveniles emerge from their burrows. Burrow entrances were observed continuously for periods of 2 to 35 hours with low light and regular video cameras. Disturbances to their burrow entrances by other fish and a large octopus caused only a temporary break in their cleaning activity. Heads of adults emerged the most (1/3 of total length) and stayed out longest (1/2 min) when they were not cleaning out their burrows but appeared to look around or lunge at other fishes. They may cannibalize their young as food. The swimming and feeding behavior of juvenile P. leucotaenia (sometimes called "mimic catfish") do not resemble that of the venomous catfish, Plotosus lineatus. Sixteen reefs were surveyed at Guadalcanal, and the Florida, Russell, and New Georgia islands. P. leucotaenia were found in all except the isolated St. Marys Island.

23756: Marine fish assemblages may be viewed as being structured by deterministic or chaotic processes. To understand factors important in structuring an assemblage of four blenniid species (Family: Blenniidae) I collected data on their abundance and distribution in early July 1997 on six offshore petroleum platforms. Hurricane Danny passed through the study area 50 km offshore of the Louisiana coast in mid July. Between late August and mid-September I collected data on nine platforms in the same area. I conducted visual censuses on diagonal cross-members of the platforms at depths of 1, 5, 10, and 15 m. Blennies displayed a distinct vertical zonation with Scartella cristata confined to the upper 2 m and Parablennius marmoreus limited to 10-15 m depths. I used Morisita's index (Im) to investigate blenniid assemblage similarity among platforms and the effect of the hurricane. Im values were compared to a null model of randomly generated data. Platforms were similar in assemblage structure with three of the four depths sampled having average Im's > 1. Pre- and post-hurricane Im's averaged greater than one in three of the four depths sampled, indicating that this disturbance did not affect these blenniid assemblages.

23757: I studied near-shore, juvenile reef fishes associated with floating objects along the Pacific coast of Panama. Using naturally-occurring flotsam and Fish Aggregation Devices (FADs), I made observations and conducted experiments on factors affecting group size and species composition. Increased FAD size and the presence of fouling biota positively affected aggregation sizes and the number of fish species present. FADs hung with model fish, lead weights and unmanipulated control FADs did not differ significantly in aggregation size or composition. However, drifting FADs deployed with live fish (Abudefduf troschelii) appeared to recruit additional fish more than those deployed without fish. The species composition of aggregations associated with drifting flotsam differed from aggregations found with anchored flotsam and anchored FADs. At an array of anchored FADs, species composition was predictable over days to weeks, but showed distinct changes over a period of months.

23758: The phylogenetic intra-relationships of esocoid fishes have been examined repeatedly in systematic studies with contradictory results. The pre-Tertiary origin of the group and low Recent diversity likely contribute to the apparent paucity of apomorphic characters that define esocoid clades. Currently, the Esocoidei contains two families, the Esocidae and Umbridae, with Esox coextensive with Esocidae, and Dallia, Novumbra, and Umbra comprising the Umbridae. Generally, the following inter-generic relationships are accepted: (Esox (Novumbra (Dallia, Umbra))), but the literature abounds with conflicting evidence. Phylogenetic analyses of DNA sequence data from the 16S rRNA and cytochrome b mitochondrial genes strongly support a previously overlooked hypothesis of esocoid relationships. Parsimony and maximum likelihood analyses show a paraphyletic Umbridae in the following set of esocoid relationships: (Umbra (Dallia (Novumbra, Esox))). Published studies of esocoid karyotypes, allozymes, and fossils offer supporting evidence for the DNA-derived hypothesis. A survey of published data on esocoid anatomy may reveal previously unrecognized morphological synapomorphies to diagnose the newly postulated clades.

23759: Goodeine fishes are remarkable for the degree to which they provision developing embryos. A suite of physiological and morphological traits permits internal fertilization, pronounced matrotrophy, and live birth in this natural group from the central plateau of Mexico. Morphological and nucleic acid sequence (COI) data form the basis of a phylogenetic analysis of goodeid interrelationships. Forty-one species from 18 genera comprise the ingroup, and members of the Cyprinodontidae, Fundulidae, Poeciliidae, Profundulidae, and Oxyzygonectes are utilized as outgroups to polarize character states. Monophyly of the Goodeidae, and the sister-group relationship of the Goodeinae and Empetrichthyinae, is supported. The Profundulidae is supported as the sister-group to the Goodeidae. Early diversification events within the Goodeinae are not well supported, potentially indicating rapid radiation of the major lineages. The evolution and biogeography of the Goodeidae will be discussed.

23760: Variation in trophic morphology is widespread in teleosts. The sources of this variation have been explored in a number of studies, and the genetic and environmental basis for extreme variation have been identified in a variety of fish. Here, I address the role development plays in producing phenotypic variation in a putative species complex of the Bahamian pupfish Cyprinodon. This taxon offers an excellent opportunity to address the origin of morphological variation in closely related species, because sympatrically occurring Cyprinodon exhibit a striking diversity in feeding morphology and behavior, yet putative species show only partial reproductive isolation. Offspring from three species and their hybrids were bred in the lab, and ontogenetic trajectories of their feeding morphology were followed until maturity. In Cyprinodon, very small differences in growth rates translate into large differences in feeding morphology. This developmental program has implications for large-scale, macroevolutionary patterns.

23761: The systematics and taxonomic history of the genus Sorubim (Teleostei: Pimelodidae) is unclear because of confusing and inadequate descriptive taxonomic literature. To assess the taxonomic status of species in the genus, I examined 347 specimens for morphological variation, including analysis of morphometry, meristics, osteology, and pigmentation throughout the known geographic range. An extensive literature review of the ten named species allocated to Sorubim and analysis of morphological data support the recognition of four species: Sorubim lima, widespread in the Amazon, Parana, and Orinoco basins; S. elongatus n. sp., occurring in the Essequibo, Orinoco, and upper Amazon drainages; S. caudacuspis n. sp., endemic to the Rio Magdalena and Lago Maracaibo drainages in Northwestern South America; and S. trigonocephalus, known only from the Rio Tapajos region in Brazil. The taxonomic revision presented includes a redescription of the genus, recognition of two nominal species as valid, descriptions of two new species, a dichotomous key, and distributional data for all nominal forms. Because of the small sample sizes available for S. trigonocephalus, future study of this species is warranted. All species of Sorubim are significant components of the ornamental fish trade and frequently found in local markets as a source of subsistence protein.

23762: The superfamily Poecilioidea contains approximately 300 species of fishes in two families, the Anablepidae (13 spp.) and the Poeciliidae (approx. 287 spp.). The monophyly of this superfamily has been supported by previous studies using morphology and DNA sequence data. However, the phylogenetic relationships within the group have been controversial. This phylogenetic analysis of over 90 transformation series and 30 representative poecilioid species supports the monophyly of the two included families. The poeciliine tribes Heterandrini, Poeciliini, and Cnesterodontini as traditionally recognized are shown to be nonmonophyletic. The facultatively viviparous species Tomeurus gracilis is nested within the poeciliine tribe Cnesterodontini and represents an evolutionary loss of obligate viviparity. Based on the phylogeny, the genus Aplocheilichthys should be restricted to the type species, Aplocheilichthys spilauchen, and Micropanchax should be recognized as the valid genus for most of the species previously placed in Aplocheilichthys. The evolution of viviparity and pelagic lacustrine habits in this group will be discussed.

23763: Snubnose darters are a fascinating group of fishes in the genus Etheostoma; breeding males exhibit some of the most fantastic colors found in North American fishes. The results of an analysis of complete cytochrome b DNA sequences (1140 base pairs) for 32 species of snubnose darters and putative close relatives are presented. Topologies obtained with parsimony, distance, and maximum likelihood criteria are congruent. The phylogenetic hypothesis supports relationships within snubnose darters that are corroborated with other evidence, although it differs from previous hypotheses in basal relationships. The cytochrome b gene tree suggests that snubnose darters are polyphyletic, with members of the subgenus Etheostoma s.s. related to one clade, and that members of the E. variatum species group are not closely related to snubnose darters or to Etheostoma s.s. The phylogeny is used for studying the evolution of several male breeding color characters that were coded and mapped onto the tree, and sexual selection experiments determined that these breeding colors were important to male reproductive success. This combination of evidence is used to propose a role for sexual selection in the differentiation of snubnose darter lineages and species.

23764: The perciform suborder Gobioidei contains an estimated 2000 species in 270 genera, found throughout the world oceans and freshwaters. This lineage is very diverse and reductive evolution is common, making traditional morphological systematic studies particularly difficult. In an attempt to resolve relationships among gobioid groups, I sequenced a 2022 base pair fragment of the mitochondrial genome, comprising the entire ND1 and ND2 genes for 40 gobioid species and performed phylogenetic analysis using cladistic parsimony methods. My data set includes representatives of the Gobiidae (including all subfamilies: Gobiinae, Gobionellinae, Oxudercinae, Amblyopinae and Sicydiinae), Microdesmidae (both subfamilies: Microdesminae and Ptereleotrinae), Kraemeriidae and Schindleriidae; representatives of the Eleotrididae were used as outgroup taxa. Analysis of the nucleotide data yielded a single phylogeny for which Bremer support and jackknife indices indicated weaker support in the deeper nodes. Analysis of translated amino acid data yielded two phylogenies differing only in the placement of one taxon; this phylogeny is congruent in many respects with gobioid relationships suggested by morphological characters. My analysis provides a broad view of gobioid relationships and, in particular, provides evidence for the relationships of the paedomorphic Kraemeriidae and Schindleriidae within the Gobioidei.

23765: The monophyly of the rhamphichthyoid gymnotiforms is supported by previous phylogenetic studies of gymnotiform fishes. In contrast, the status and relationships of the constituent subgroups of the rhamphichthyoids remain poorly understood. The goal of this work was to determine whether the currently recognized rhamphichthyoid taxa represent monophyletic groups and to ascertain the species-level relationships among them, with special emphasis on the Family Hypopomidae Mago-Leccia, 1976. An additional goal was to gain insight into the evolution of the species-specific electric organ discharge (EOD). A phylogenetic study of 23 rhamphichthyoid species was carried out based on mitochondrial DNA sequence data from the portions of the 12S rRNA, 16S rRNA and cytochrome b genes and a morphological data set. Results indicate that nominal hypopomid genera Steatogenys and Hypopygus do not form a clade with other nominal hypopomids but strongly support the monophyly of the remaining nominal hypopomids. Additionally, the nominal species of Brachyhypopomus form a clade with five new species. Genus Brachyhypopomus is the sister taxon to the monotypic genus Microstemarchus which together form the sister group to genus Hypopomus. Complex EODs and a monophasic EOD appear to have arisen within the Hypopomidae independently of these character states in outgroup taxa.

23766: The Amphiprioninae is a subfamily of marine fishes, commonly called anemonefishes, composed of two genera (Amphiprion and Premnas) with approximately 28 species. The phylogenetic relationships within this subfamily are poorly understood. Although a hypothetical set of relationships has been previously proposed, the phylogeny of the group has never been fully examined. Previous work has suggested that the members of this subfamily are divided among six species complexes. At least one representative species from all six of these complexes and three outgroup (pomacentrid) genera were examined. Morphological characters, primarily osteological ones, were used to conduct a phylogenetic analysis of this subfamily. The preliminary results will be presented and evolution of the fish-anemone relationship will be discussed.

23767: Hypotheses concerning modes of allopatric speciation make explicit predictions regarding patterns of phylogenetic and biogeographic diversification. This investigation will test allopatric speciation models using phylogenetic and biogeographic information for the subgenus Swainia, a monophyletic group of four described species in the genus Percina. Complete gene sequences of the mitochondrially encoded cytochrome b have been collected from all species of Swainia, including individuals from multiple populations of P. phoxocephala and P. nasuta. Patterns of nucleotide variation were investigated and phylogenetic relationships were estimated using maximum parsimony, maximum likelihood, and distance optimality criteria. Heterogeneity of nucleotide substitution rate was examined using both maximum parsimony relative rate tests and a likelihood ratio test. Inferred phylogenetic relationships, biogeographic patterns, and relative amounts of nucleotide divergence are used to develop hypotheses of speciation in Swainia.
23768: This presentation is part of a wider study of the biogeography of Australian freshwater fishes. Southeastern Australia is hereby defined as coastal drainages from the Fitzroy River through Gulf of St. Vincent, including the inland Murray system separated from coastal drainages by the Great Dividing Range. It has the following biogeographic relationships of fishes restricted to freshwater: 1) 5 of 8 species from southern Victoria also occur in the Murray system; and 2) 18 of 27 species (or species pairs) co-occur between coastal Queensland drainages and the Murray system. The relationships of an additional 6 species endemic to the Murray system are more obscure. Biogeographic connectivity between the Murray and surrounding drainages thus appears high. Past biogeographic explanations for these relationships have relied heavily upon river captures, making faunal distributions easily explained. However, the last 15 years have seen a paradigm shift in the proposed evolution of the Great Dividing Range including evidence that river captures are either non-existent or very old (> 30-60 mya). Most patterns are congruent with present geological scenarios although exceptions exist. The new geologic conclusions are assessed on the basis of biological evidence and new hypotheses are provided to explain present distribution patterns.

23769: Phylogenetic relationships of the endemic Malagasy cichlids were investigated using DNA sequence data and combined evidence. Prior attempts based on morphological evidence to generate a highly supported and resolved phylogenetic hypothesis have been only partially successful, and this lack of resolution has been attributed to muted anatomical variation and a high degree of convergence/parallelism within Cichlidae. DNA sequence data is presented corresponding to two regions of the mitochondrial genome for a representative sampling of cichlid taxa, including all of the known Malagasy cichlids. The use of molecular sequence data results in a highly resolved phylogenetic hypothesis for Cichlidae. However, support for higher-level relationships is relatively weak, and may indicate that differentiation in ancient cichlid lineages occurred over a relatively short time. Results based on DNA sequence data indicate that the Malagasy cichlids (including the Asian genera) are not monophyletic, that the Etropline cichlids (Etroplus from India/Sri Lanka and Paretroplus from Madagascar) form a natural group, and that the Ptychochromine cichlids (including Oxylapia) are a monophyletic Malagasy assemblage. Biogeography of the Malagasy cichlids, and Cichlidae in general, will also be discussed.

23770: An amphibian survey was initiated at Brazos Bend State Park, Fort Bend County, Texas to assess anecdotal observations of anuran population declines. From February to July 1997, 12 amphibian species were documented at the park. Sixty-nine sites used by amphibians were identified, of which 73% contained evidence of breeding. It does not appear that amphibian species are in decline at Brazos Bend State Park. In February 1998, 350 meters of PVC pipe were installed at selected sites to evaluate the effectiveness of this technique in regard to hylid frog populations. These and other sites are currently being monitored in order to gain insight to amphibian population dynamics at Brazos Bend State Park.
23771: Apparent declines of amphibian populations in many parts of the world have caused great concern in recent years. This study was conducted to determine what effects agriculturally induced fragmentation of forests has had on amphibian assemblages and their distribution in a midwestern landscape. Potential breeding pools and upland areas in 30 forest patches of various sizes and degrees of isolation were intensively sampled for amphibians from April through August 1996 and March through August 1997. Species presence was documented by using pitfall trapping, anuran vocalization surveys, cover board sampling, minnow traps, and dipnetting for larva. Amphibian, anuran and salamander assemblages were all nonrandomly distributed across the landscape. Bufo americanus and Hyla versicolor were ubiquitous whereas the distribution of several species including Ambystoma tigrinum, A. texanum, Plethodon cinereus, Rana clamitans, and R. pipiens showed significant nesting. Overall, species richness was significantly associated with a weighted measure of wetland permanency (WETWGT, p=0.0001, WETWGTC2, p=0.0029), with forest patches which have seasonal and semi-permanent wetlands containing more species. Abundance of amphibians was significantly associated with forest proximity (LOGPR, p=0.0001, LOGPRC2, p=0.0037), with more isolated patches having greater amphibian abundance. The observed distribution and degree of nestedness exhibited by several amphibians suggests that these species respond to landscape-level factors.

23772: The longleaf pine ecosystem, once widespread in the southeastern United States, has been reduced by as much as 98%. Restoration of this endangered ecosystem can be a mechanism for conservation, in an attempt to reverse existing damage and create more resilient communities. Restoration methods implemented in sandhills must be based in a deep knowledge of the ecosystem to effectively recreate and manage all aspects. Consequently, restoration success can only be evaluated by examining community response. Since reptiles and amphibians occupy the ecosystem at a fairly small scale, these communities may be important indicators of microhabitat restoration success. Previous work on herpetofaunal response to disturbance regimes has demonstrated the complexity of the effects and the importance of habitat structure. Habitat requirements for sandhill herpetofauna are very diverse, demonstrating the need to closely examine these communities when making management decisions. My study, focused on reptiles and amphibians, is one portion of a multi-agency investigation of three sandhill restoration techniques on Eglin Air Force Base, Florida: fire, oak-specific herbicide, and mechanical oak felling. Pitfall traps and drift fences were used to capture reptiles and amphibians in restoration treatment areas, control plots and 'typical' longleaf pine sandhill areas during the summer of 1997. Animals were identified to species, marked, sexed, weighed, measured, and visually examined. Vegetative cover data were also collected. The objective of this project is to examine herpetofaunal species richness and abundance, as well as population age class structure and sex ratios, with regards to the restoration treatment and vegetative structure.

23773: Alberta-Pacific Forest Industries Inc. (AL-PAC) operates a large pulp mill in the mixed-wood boreal forest of northeastern Alberta. The company harvests within its 6,000,000 ha Forest Management Area (FMA) using an 'ecosystem management' perspective. In other words, AL-PAC attempts to mimic fire, the dominant natural disturbance of the boreal forest. Five amphibian species, including two that appear to have undergone population declines, occur in the FMA. In 1997, I sampled anuran communities at 12 lakes to investigate whether each species showed the same relative abundance in logged, naturally burned, and undisturbed areas. I employed call surveys, transect sampling, egg and larval searches, and metamorph searches. Additionally, I conducted vegetation surveys on each transect to quantitatively examine differences in habitat. Preliminary results suggest that lakes with adjacent cutblocks support the highest number of amphibians; however, this may be a function of lake size, distance from active roads, or forest type. An analysis to separate these effects is underway.

23774: Human activities tend to create highly fragmented landscapes, thereby exposing animal populations to edges. I am interested in the impacts of forest-pasture edges on the dynamics of frog and lizard populations. Using a paired-plot design I described the abundance and distribution of lizards (Norops spp.) and leaf-litter frogs (Eleutherodactylus spp.) in 10 forest fragments near Las Cruces, Costa Rica. The study took place from February to June 1997 and covered both dry and wet seasons. No species was definitively absent from the edge plots. Nocturnal leaf-litter frogs were generally equally abundant near forest edges and in forest interiors. The single diurnal eleutherodactylid species, however, was consistently more abundant in the forest interiors, suggesting that edge effects may be stronger during the day than at night. Anoline lizards were more abundant at the edges during the dry season but became more abundant in forest interiors during the wet season. This seasonal variation adds a new dimension to our understanding of edge effects, and carries important practical implications for future studies. The reproductive period of the lizards, which coincides with the rainy season, as well as lower rates of parasitism on anoline lizards near edges, are offered as possible explanations for the observed seasonal pattern.

23775: Terrestrial salamanders spend the majority of their time in cool, moist refugia underground, but must surface to forage and breed. Although little is known about their surface activity patterns, abundance is usually inferred by counts of surface active salamanders on wet nights. Recently, such counts have been used to assess the impacts of timber harvesting on terrestrial salamanders. It is assumed in these studies that the percent of the population active on the surface is not altered by the treatment. We tested this assumption by conducting a mark-recapture study on harvested and control plots. We found significantly different proportions active between treatments. At one location, the harvested plot had a lower percent active than its control (Plethodon cinereus: 4.0% vs. 9.2%, p=.021; P. glutinosus: 3.8% vs. 11.7%, p=.091). At the other location, the harvested plots had a higher percent active than their controls (P. cinereus: 4.2% and 3.9% vs. 1.6% and 1.3%, p=.017). At this site, surface counts indicated there were more salamanders on the harvested plots than on the controls, but mark-recapture estimates indicated there were actually twice as many salamanders on the control plots.

23776: Populations that experience a large reduction in effective size are expected to exhibit a bottleneck effect which will include loss of heterozygosity and loss of alleles. Populations of the southwestern pond turtle, Clemmys marmorata pallida, in Central and Southern California were impacted by an extended drought that occurred from 1987-1992 and exhibited local population size decreases up to 85% during this period. I examined changes in genetic diversity in four populations of C. marmorata in the drought affected area by comparing microsatellite DNA allele frequencies from tissue samples collected before and after this drought period. Genotypes of five microsatellite loci were determined to assess the genetic diversity within these samples. Heterozygosity was used as a measurement of genetic diversity. Although no significant decline in heterozygosity was shown in the five loci, there was a decrease in the number of alleles present in the most severely impacted population. Since most individuals that were present in the post-drought samples were survivors of the drought, the first sign of decreased genetic diversity would be the loss of alleles. Changes in the level of genetic diversity (heterozygosity) would only be detectable in subsequent post-drought generations.

23778: The geographic range of the gopher tortoise has declined due to habitat destruction and fragmentation. Protection strategies typically include preserving patches of habitat or conserving areas occupied by tortoises, even if those areas are restricted in size and quality. However, the patterns observed in these sites can differ from those in large, contiguous areas where conditions may more closely resemble those under which the species evolved. We tracked 131 tortoises via radio-telemetry for one year on an 11,700 ha longleaf pine reserve in southwest Georgia. Male tortoises utilized an average of 9.3 + 4.6 burrows and traveled an average total distance of 83.7 + 73.8 m during the study period. Females utilized 4.8 ± 2.4 burrows and traveled 48.2 ± 57.7 m. The longest movements were 6.4 km by a male tortoise and 480 m by a female. The results of this study emphasize the need to preserve large, contiguous habitats for use by gopher tortoises. Furthermore, it suggests that movement by tortoises is limited in small habitats, especially those surrounded by vast inhospitable areas. Data gathered within large study sites may provide better information for the long-term preservation of this species.

23779: Mitochondrial DNA sequence analyses were used to infer phylogeographic relationships among individuals of the lizard species Cnemidophorus sexlineatus, as well as to determine whether a population of C. sexlineatus in Michigan is endemic or recently introduced. Individuals were obtained from Colorado, Oklahoma, Indiana, Michigan, and Florida. A PCR generated fragment which spans the mtDNA ND3 to ND4 gene region, and including the Arginine tRNA, was sequenced for each individual. Sceloporus grammicus and C. gularis sequences were used as outgroups. The preliminary data cannot rule out the possibility that the Michigan population is endemic. The Florida individuals are in a clade basal to a clade that contains Michigan, Indiana, and Oklahoma individuals. Sequence divergence values of the Michigan specimens range from 1.2% to 5.8%. The Indiana and Oklahoma specimens have sequence divergence values of 1.6% to 2.3% and 1.1% to 1.5% respectively. One Colorado sample forms a clade with the C. gularis sample, its sequence divergence is 8.3%.

23780: Peatlands are increasingly exploited in Europe and North America due to the demand for peat in horticulture. As a result, these wetlands are threatened, particularly in New Brunswick and Quebec, North America's principal peat producers. I used drift fences and pitfall traps to investigate amphibian populations in pristine bogs and disturbed bogs (i.e., bog remnants adjacent to peat harvesting operations) of southeastern New Brunswick. Results following 20,592 trap nights indicate that species richness is higher in pristine bogs than disturbed bogs (range 2-7 spp.). Rana clamitans was the only species sensitive to peat harvesting, while the abundance of Rana sylvatica, Rana pipiens, Bufo americanus americanus and Rana septentrionalis did not differ between pristine bogs and bog fragments. Captured individuals consisted almost exclusively of ranid juveniles in both types of bogs. These data show that peat bog harvesting has a definite influence on adjacent amphibian communities. However, additional work will be needed to differentiate natural population fluctuations from the impacts of peat harvesting on amphibian movements and resource (i.e., bog ponds) utilization.

23781: For amphibians that breed in temporary pools, juvenile dispersal is an important life history movement linking the aquatic habitat of larvae to the surrounding forest habitat occupied by most adults. We examined whether selection occurs for closed-canopy conditions during dispersal using pitfall traps and drift fences to sample naturally occurring, upland populations of wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) and spotted salamanders (Ambystoma maculatum) along recently created forest-clearcut edges in central Maine. Habitat preferences during dispersal were further investigated using an experimental approach that quantified the movements of newly metamorphosed wood frogs cultured in artificial pools located along an abrupt forest-powerline edge. Among natural populations the abundance of juveniles and adults of both species declined sharply across a gradient running from relatively mature forest-interior habitat (70-90 years old) to recently clearcut habitat (2-11 years old). Similarly, in the powerline experiment, juvenile wood frogs showed a dispersal preference for closed-canopy habitat immediately upon metamorphosis, with the highest capture rates occurring in microhabitats characterized by dense foliage in both the understory and canopy layers. Our results suggest that populations of wood frogs, spotted salamanders, and other vernal pool breeding amphibian species are likely to benefit from efforts to maintain connectivity between upland forest habitats and aquatic breeding sites.

23782: Bison wallows and intermittent streams were sampled weekly in spring 1996 and 1997 on Konza Prairie Research Natural Area, Kansas. We monitored water chemistry and development of western chorus frogs (Pseudacris triseriata) as these aquatic habitats dried. Abiotic factors temporally were more variable in bison wallows than in intermittent streams even after flow stopped. Dissolved oxygen and ammonium fluctuated diurnally in wallows, but remained stable in intermittent streams until just before drying. Water temperature and pH were correlated negatively to water volume in wallows, but not in streams. Eggs in bison wallows hatched at Gosner stages 21 and 22 within 4 to 8 days after laying, whereas eggs in intermittent streams hatched in 14 days at about Gosner stage 21. The majority of tadpoles in wallows reached Gosner stages 38 to 42 in 6 weeks, when wallows dried. In contrast, tadpole development in streams progressed no further than stage 25 until flow ceased in streams, and no tadpoles developed beyond stage 41 when the streams dried after 16 weeks. Differences in developmental rates of these frogs likely result from differences in water temperature and chemistry between ephemeral aquatic habitats found in wallows and streams.

23783: The post-breeding migration of Rana temporaria was studied by means of radio tracking over three years. One site consisted of an extensive ungrazed, uncut moist meadow where suitable foraging habitats and the breeding site were all contiguous with each other, while in another site suitable habitats were separated by cultivated fields. The study period of the first year coincided with a drought, while the study periods of the following two years had above normal precipitation. This enabled a factorial analysis of the effects of seasonal weather, landscape type and sex on migratory behavior. In the farmland site and during the wet years frogs moved farther from their breeding pond and sources of open water, changed position more often and made longer movements when position was changed. In the farmland site frogs also migrated farther and did so more directly. Nearly all differences between sites were more noticeable during the wet year. There were no significant differences between the sexes, neither were any of the differences between habitats or wet and dry years sex dependent. These migration patterns are discussed in terms of the effects of habitat fragmentation on species survival and the consequences for dispersal between breeding populations.

23784: The influence of weather on salamander breeding activity has been well documented. However, weather influence on specific movement patterns is not yet well understood. I investigated the influence of weather variables on movements of Northwestern salamanders. Radio-tracking was conducted during the winter when this species is most active. Both non-breeding and breeding migration movements were observed. Movements were significantly correlated with both temperature increase and rain onset. This relationship was strongest when a cold, dry period was followed by a warm, wet period. Movements began when daily temperatures rose above a mean of 5°C and a minimum of 0°C, and more than 20mm of rain had fallen within the last 24 hours. During these periods most radio-tagged salamanders moved within 48 hours of the weather change and of each other. Breeding migration movements were also correlated with this type of weather change and migration onset invariably began within 48 hours of the first winter thaw. Subsequent cold, dry periods were observed to temporarily suspend migrational movements. During extended periods of warm rainy weather, correlations between weather variables and movements were much weaker and tended to be better explained by individual salamander movement frequency patterns.

23785: Nitrogen pollution from anthropogenic sources enters water bodies through runoff associated with nitrate fertilization, livestock, precipitation, and effluents from industrial, human and animal wastes. This review assesses the potential for nitrate to affect amphibian populations by comparing environmental concentrations of nitrate in North American waters to nitrate concentrations known to cause toxicity to captive amphibians and other species that play an important role in amphibian ecology. Lethal and sublethal effects in amphibians are detected at nitrate concentrations between 2.5 and 100 mg/L. We found environmental concentrations of nitrate in watersheds throughout North America from <1 to >100 mg/L. Furthermore, amphibian food (insects) and predators (fish) are also affected by these elevated levels of nitrate in surface waters. From this we conclude that nitrate concentrations in watersheds in North America are high enough to cause death and developmental anomalies in amphibians. In the interim, use of vegetated buffer strips adjacent to water courses can reduce nitrogen contamination of surface waters. Ultimately, there is a need to reduce the use of fertilizers, control the run-off of human and livestock waste and establish and enforce water quality guidelines for nitrate for the protection of aquatic life.

23786: The floodplain area of 32 lakes in Lower Solimões River (Amazon) was quantified using a radar image SAR (JERS-1) in order to stablish correlations among these areas and the catch per unit of effort - CPUE (total and by species) in the lakes (effort unit = fisherman numbers x fishery days). Results showed correlation between the lake area and its floodplain area (n=32; Pearson r; p<0.05) while there was a weak correlation of meander number and lakes floodplain area (n=32; r=0.4, ns), and the lake perimeter was correlated with all variables. Catch data shows that just CPUE total was correlated with the floodplain area (Spearman r=0.69; p<0.05; n=8). Lacustrine species and riverine-lacustrine species did not show correlation with the others variables (floodplain area, lake area, perimeter and meander number). However, since Amazon fishes distribution is dependent on many others variables (floodplain forest size and diversity, ecosystem primary production, etc.) those correlations need to be investigated based on larger sample size in order to determinate standards.

23787: Billings reservoir (127 km2, 23° 42' - 23° 45'S; 46° 27' - 46° 22'W) is the largest water body in the metropolitan region of São Paulo (Brazil). Its building started in 1925 in order to supply the city of São Paulo with electricity. During many years it presented low environmental quality due to the reception of organic sewage from the metropolitan region. Nowadays, it has multiple uses. An intense artisanal fishery activity is present, with 191 fishermen. Landings were recorded daily during a year (1996). During this period 147,593 kg of fish were caught in 3,515 fishing trips by 21.5 fishermen/month in average, with a yield of 42 kg/trip and 572 kg/fisherman/month. The main commercial species caught were Nile tilapia Oreochromis niloticus (81.4% of landings in weight), an introduced species, 'lambari' Astyanax eigenmanniorum (13.0%) and four other species. Tilapias were caught with castnets and beating gillnets, the other species were caught with gillnets. Through a Principal Component Analysis it was possible to detect two main groups of fishermen considering the fisheries strategies, those who explore only tilapias and those who explore also the other species, related mainly to the ownership of the gears. The low richness and high dominance of few species on landings are indicative of communities under stressing condition. The dominance of Nile tilapia is attributable to a combination of factors as ability to consume plankton and tolerance to low dissolved oxygen contents. 23788: Floodplain fishes in the mid-upper Rio Negro are exploited as ornamental fishes to provide subsistence to 3000 people in Barcelos, Amazonas (pop. 12,000; area 122,490 km2). Turtles and their eggs are the second most important protein resource, next to fish. This fishery constitutes over 60% of the economic activity of the region. About 60 species and 20 million fishes are captured for the trade annually. A single species, the cardinal tetra (Paracheirodon axelrodi), made up more than 70% of the catch. Over fishing in some areas may be attributed to lack of rural employment since other extractive economies have collapsed. Thus more people are involved in the fishery. El Niño, now, as in 1982-3, is probably the principal cause of the drastic decline of the fishery. Our goals are to understand the biology of this community so that a management plan can be devised to use these resources on a sustainable level. To accomplish these goals we are studying the biodiversity and biology of the species of fish used in the ornamental fish trade, the turtles used as food and trade, and the social-economic aspects of this fishery. It may be possible to use this resource as well as preserve it.
23789: Selective timber harvesting (removal of individual trees or small groups of trees), which creates gaps in the forest canopy, is widely practiced in public and private forests. However, the effects of this technique on herpetofaunal populations has been incompletely studied. We examined the effect of forest canopy gaps, created by selective harvesting, on the distribution of the northern redback salamander, Plethodon cinereus, in a maple-hemlock forest in central New York State. Distributions of individual salamanders were determined by searching 1 m x 1 m quadrats along transects extending from the center of gaps into the surrounding forest. In the first year following harvest, we found that salamander distributions did not indicate significant movement from or avoidance of gap sites. However, salamander densities were somewhat elevated on the edges of gaps. Data for the second year following harvest are being analyzed.

23790: We entered citation information for all natural history and geographic distribution records from Herpetological Review (HR), from its first issues to the present. Citations include authors, species, keywords, and locality information. The HR database is available to anyone with WWW access, and can be searched in a variety of ways. This makes preliminary literature research much quicker and more thorough than was previously possible. For example, when a herpetologist finds a specimen believed to be new for a county, it is now easy to determine if the species has already been reported for that region in HR. The HR database will be updated continually as new issues become available. As an example of the value of this database, we examined new county record data for a collection of species (Rana catesbeiana, Hemidactylus turcicus, and Trachemys scripta) that are commonly introduced to new areas outside their native range. The results show the pattern of range expansion differs among the three species.

23791: The south-west coast of Australia (Darling Botanical District), as defined by the 800mm isohyet, has an area of some 160,000 square kilometres and 19 distinct river drainage basins. In comparison to habitats of southeastern Australia and the Northern Hemisphere, southwestern Australia has a much reduced aquatic faunal diversity: the freshwaters of this region contain only 10 species of native fishes, of which eight are endemic. With the exception of Tandanus bostocki (a freshwater catfish) none of these species typically exceed 140mm in total length. This very low number of freshwater fish species in southwestern Australian waters is thought to be a result of the regions arid past climate, insular nature, low and relatively featureless topography, and low productivity of its aquatic habitats. The regions recreational freshwater fishery currently comprises the introduced perch (Perca fluviatilis) and trouts (Salmo trutta, Oncorhynchus mykiss), and the native decapod, Cherax tenuimanus, the third largest freshwater crayfish. Preliminary data suggests the temperate climate of the south-west promotes fast growth-rates of perch, yet shortens the period during which their spawning is successful, relative to Northern Hemisphere populations. This paper also discusses the likely impact of P. fluviatilis on the established C. tenuimanus fishery, given that at times P. fluviatilis preys almost exclusively on this crayfish species.
23792: The New York State Department of Environmental Conservation has been directing the NY Amphibian and Reptile Atlas, a state-wide, ten-year survey of the herpetofaunal populations which relies heavily on volunteer participation. Using an SSAR grant-in-aid-of-herpetology for education, we initiated a project to increase the educational value of the Atlas for young people and to increase their participation as contributors. To encourage participation, biology teachers in over 70 high schools were contacted directly with information about the project. Other teachers were reached via a museum exhibit at SUNY Cortland and a web page. The web page (www.cortland.edu/herp/) contains identification keys and photographs of local species, information about the Atlas, and web resource links. Participating high school classes also received educational packets containing frog call tapes, books to aid field identification, field survey tips, Atlas handbooks and newsletters, and information on herpetofaunal conservation. Students from across the state are now participating.

23793: In 1992, the Canadian government passed amendments to the Pulp and Paper Effluent Regulations (PPER) under the Fisheries Act, which included a requirement for mills to conduct an Environmental Effects Monitoring (EEM) program. The purpose of EEM is to assess the adequacy of national regulations for protecting fish, fish habitat and the use of fisheries resources. One key component of EEM is a fish survey (FS), which involves sampling two sentinel species from an exposure area and examining gross population characteristics. EEM requirements specify growth, reproduction and survival as key assessment endpoints for fish. The primary objective of the first survey (Cycle 1) was to determine variability in the measured parameters and determine sample sizes using power analysis for subsequent cycles. Following the completion of Cycle 1, a number of refinements to the EEM program have been implemented. The purpose of this paper is to review the changes to the FS component of EEM and discuss the use of the FS data in decision making. Difficulties with the FS component and alternative approaches to the fish survey (e.g., mesocosms) currently being explored will also be presented.

23794: Avon Park Air Force Range is a federal military reservation occupying 42,900 hectares in Florida's Greater Everglades Region. Prior to this study, the area was one of the more poorly sampled sites for fishes in all of central Florida. In addition to bomb craters, aquatic habitats include the Kissimmee River canal and associated remnant meander channels; Lake Arbuckle (1550 ha); several small lakes; blackwater streams; extensive marshes; hardwood, cypress and pine swamps; cattle ponds; and ditches. As part of an aquatic faunal survey (1995-1997), we documented presence of 44 fish species (representing 17 fish families), eight nonindigenous, and one nonindigenous clam and two native crayfishes. Introduced foreign species captured in the area included walking catfish (Clarias batrachus), blue tilapia (Oreochromis aureus), grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella) and Asian clam Corbicula fluminea. Two natives, eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki) and least killifish (Heterandria formosa), were by far the most abundant and widespread fishes. Compared with much of Florida, anthropogenic impacts range from low to moderate (e.g., cattle throughout, water diversion in some sections, periodic artillery fire in a few areas). Relative to many environments in peninsular Florida, numbers and densities of nonindigenous fishes in the range are low.

23795: Diet and feeding habits of the smooth dogfish (Mustelus canis), Atlantic sharpnose shark (Rhizoprionodon terranovae), dusky shark (Carcharhinus obscurus) and the sand tiger (Carcharias taurus) were investigated through analysis of stomach contents. Diet in M. canis was relatively homogeneous and was dominated by crustaceans, consisting mostly of rock crabs, Cancer irroratus. Diet in R. terranovae was more heterogeneous and consisted largely of crustaceans and teleosts, in similar levels of prey importance. Use of cumulative prey curves as a measure of precision indicated that data was insufficient to fully describe the diets of C. obscurus and C. taurus. Nonetheless, these data suggested that both species are generalized feeders and consume a variety of teleost and elasmobranch prey. Further studies are necessary to fully characterize diet in these two species. In addition, more data are necessary to examine ontogenetic, seasonal and substrate-related shifts in diet for all of the species investigated.

23796: Long-term field studies of sexual selection in the explosively breeding American toad, Bufo americanus, reveal only weak evidence of non-random mating based on size. Although advantages may accrue to females that breed with larger males, levels of male-male competition and opportunities for female choice vary. High levels of natal philopatry predict that close inbreeding should be common. Genetic analyses suggest to the contrary that: (1) in natural populations toads largely avoid close inbreeding, and (2) males' advertisement calls encode information about their genetic identities. To examine whether females can assess their relatedness to males by hearing their calls, I conducted laboratory playback experiments. The responses of female subjects to males' calls, broadcast alternately, were analysed as a function of their relatedness to each of the males (determined by multilocus DNA fingerprinting). Females discriminated between calls based on kinship, consistently orienting toward calls of the genetically less similar male. Responses were similar to field-recorded calls and to synthesised calls (controlling for call duration and number of pulses). Females showed no preference if equally related to each calling male. These results suggest that mate choice is more strongly influenced by selection to avoid close inbreeding than by sexual selection for other characters.

23797: Studies employing historical methods have shown that preexisting biases in the sensory systems of females are capable of driving the evolution of male traits. I used artificial neural network models - computer simulations emulating real nervous systems - to test whether receiver biases could be directly influenced by the evolutionary history of the female sensory apparatus. Neural networks were given an evolutionary history approximating that of the tungara frog, or one of various control histories. I found that not only does evolutionary history influence receiver biases, but that networks with a history approximating that of the tungara frog were best at predicting female responses to many novel heterospecific calls. The neural networks demonstrate patterns of preference that are clearly vestiges of past selection pressures, and make novel predictions about the preferences of real females.

23798: We have been using the advertisement call system of tungara frogs (Physalaemus pustulosus) and their close relatives to attempt to understand the evolution of communication systems. We have analyzed the advertisement calls and phylogenetic relationships of members of the Physalaemus pustulosus species group and three other congeners as outgroups. Using these data we have estimated calls at ancestral nodes and tested tungara frog female preferences for these calls. Here we address the following questions: (1) How conservative is the evolution of various call characters; (2) How do individual call characters influence advertisement call recognition (heterospecific call versus white noise) and discrimination (heterospecific call versus conspecific call); and, (3) Does the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character differentially influence call recognition and discrimination. Our results suggest that: (1) calls do not evolve as tightly coordinated suites of characters, but instead are arrays of more or less plesiomorphic or derived characters; (2) that call discrimination and recognition might be influenced differently by some call characters than others; and, (3) that the degree of plesiomorphy of a call character might have some effect on these tasks.

23799: Visual displays are known in both intra- and intersexual anuran communication. We compare the patterns of visual signaling among seven anuran families and discuss the ecological contexts in which they may have evolved. We classified visual cues used during intraspecific interactions as discrete character states and mapped them onto a phylogenetic tree based on morphological characters. Groups of behavioural patterns are apparent and closely but not exclusively associated with anuran families. By adding ecological characteristics and geographic distributions of the involved species to the matrix, the resulting patterns suggest visual displays to be more similar between species of the same family. As striking exceptions, similar displays are performed by two across-family groups of species. Diurnal, neotropical leaf-litter inhabitants and mainly aposematic species in the Brachycephalidae, Bufonidae and Dendrobatidae exhibit an impressive variety of visual displays involving predominantly anterior parts of the body. Stream-side breeding, cryptic species in the Leptodactylidae, Myobatrachidae, Hylidae and Ranidae constitute another probably convergent group, which includes both nocturnal and diurnal species exposed to constant high ambient noise levels. They perform conspicuous visual displays by extending or 'flagging' the posterior limbs. However, Hyla parviceps and Phyllomedusa spp., which advertise and breed at ponds, perform similar displays. The observed patterns suggest that complex visual communication may have evolved under two ecological scenarios. One is associated with the shift to diurnality and the other with breeding at tropical mountain streams. (Foot-flagging displays of Hylodes asper and Staurois latopalmatus are shown in film and video scenes)

23800: Influence of time of day, location of shark and tracker experience on swimming speed was examined in seven subadult lemon sharks using speed sensing transmitters. Of nine sharks caught using long line gear between January 1997 and August 1997, seven, ranging in size from 160 cm to 183 cm, were fitted with a combination of two telemetry transmitters. The devices, a 75 kHz coded transmitter for identification and a 68 kHz transmitter for speed sensing were mated with cable ties and fixed to the shark with metal darts at the base of the first dorsal fin. The seven sharks were tracked for a total of 450 hours with at least one continuous, 24 hour track for each shark. The longest continuous track was 88 hours. Using GIS and standard statistical methods a first analysis of swimming speeds did not reveal any significant differences according to time of day. Daytime and nighttime swimming speeds averaged 0.33 body lengths per second (bl/s), while crepuscular speeds averaged 0.32 bl/s. In addition, burst-speed events did not appear to show any correlation with time of day. GIS analysis of swimming speed and shark location showed average speeds to be slightly slower in areas adjacent to mangroves. Swimming speeds were noted to decline steadily from 0.45 bl/s with the first 4 sharks tracked to a steady 0.32-0.33 bl/s for the final three sharks. This suggested that tracker experience can significantly influence the speed of a shark. Detailed analysis of the tracking continues. The bioenergetic significance of these trackings will be discussed. Supported by the US Office of Naval Research, the Bimini Biological Field Station and the Earthwatch organization.

23801: Environmental contamination with anthropogenic chemicals has been implicated in the decline and disappearance of amphibians from many localities around the world. Point Pelee National Park in southern Ontario has lost 5 of 10 amphibian species in the last 50 years. Habitat loss has occurred but cannot account for the number of amphibian extirpations documented in the park. Similar amphibian losses have not occurred at nearby wetlands. Amphibian extirpations at Point Pelee follow a period of DDT application in orchards. DDT and metabolite concentrations were greatest in terrestrial amphibians (Pseudacris crucifer and Bufo americanus) and least in aquatic amphibians (Rana clamitans and Rana pipiens). High pesticide concentrations were measured in reptilian predators of amphibians, however pesticide concentrations measured in predatory fish were much lower than in snakes of similar trophic position. Trophic magnification of pesticides was observed only in the terrestrial food web. Pesticide accumulation in amphibians was positively related to site contamination. These data collected in southern Ontario indicate that the historic use of pesticides may be an important determinant of local distribution of amphibians and their predators.

23802: This study will explore the efficiency of different inventory sampling methods for an assemblage of lowland tropical amphibians and reptiles. The goal of this research is to identify which methods give the most accurate description of a herpetofaunal assemblage. Data were collected from the Iwokrama International Centre for Rain Forest Conservation and Development in central Guyana. Four different methods (day visual encounter survey, night visual encounter survey, leaf litter plots, and opportunistic collecting) were used to examine the assemblage structure. Results will be presented examining the variation in descriptors of amphibian and reptile species diversity among different populations and different methods. It is important for researchers to develop standard methods for sampling assemblage structure. Inventory sampling provides information on assemblage structure and baseline species diversity data for future comparisons. Therefore, these data are critical in the quest to discover the relationship between species loss and ecosystem function.

23803: Counts of amphibians over time were compiled from published accounts. At the time this abstract was written, 37 studies have yielded 110 separate count series for 45 amphibian species. Counts were analyzed to determine series mean, detrended standard deviation, and subsequent coefficient of variation (CV). Studies have been categorized according to taxonomic group, sampling method, study region, and count type (index vs. population estimate). Initial analyses indicate significant differences among count CVs based on count type, with CVs from population estimates being significantly lower than index CVs (p = 0.016). While sample sizes were low, there are further indications that CVs of counts of terrestrial and stream salamanders are much lower than most anuran and pond-breeding salamanders. We are currently adding counts to the database as new studies arise. We will also demonstrate the impact of variability on power and sample size requirements for monitoring programs using the program MONITOR. Finally, we plan to use studies providing within season data and multiple site data to characterize the various components of count variance among sampling error and yearly variation.

23804: This study examined herpetofaunal assemblage structure in three floodplain habitats (broadleaf marsh, wetland forest, and wetland shrub) of the Kissimmee River. The Kissimmee River is the subject of a large-scale restoration project and its success will be evaluated by analyzing changes in the associated biotic assemblages. Data were collected for 12 consecutive months from August, 1996, to July, 1997, using nocturnal visual encounter surveys. 23805: As part of a long-term amphibian monitoring program, automated acoustical recorders were placed at five sites in two national parks in New Brunswick during the summer of 1997. Each recorder took a one minute long acoustical sample every hour from early May until the end of August, for an average of 110 recording days per recorder. Analysis of acoustical samples revealed the presence of five anuran species, Pseudacris crucifer, Rana catesbeiana, Rana clamitans, Rana sylvatica, and Bufo americanus. A sixth species, Rana pipiens, was detected on only one occasion. Three species also found in New Brunswick (Hyla versicolor, Rana palustris, and Rana septentrionalis) were not detected at any of the sampled sites. Chorus activity patterns changed over the breeding season for each species. In general, chorus activity was highest between the hours of 10 pm and 5 am, although calling individuals were frequently recorded throughout the day. We also compared two acoustical sampling protocols (one min every hour vs. 12 s every 15 min). Both strategies detected the same species richness, but showed subtle differences in anuran activity patterns. Comparison of calling activity with meteorological data is currently underway.

23806: Onondaga Lake lies in the Syracuse NY urbanization zone surrounded by industrial, commercial, and residential areas. The lake has been greatly impacted by a century of industrial waste dumping and sewage discharge. Since 1994, herpetofaunal surveys have been conducted in the lake and adjacent terrestrial and wetland areas using transects, quadrats, trapping arrays, select point sampling, and calling surveys spanning all active seasons. The Onondaga Lake ecosystem was found to support reduced herpetofaunal diversity and population sizes compared to less disturbed areas in the region. No amphibians breed in the lake itself or in any wetland with direct connections to the lake. Five anuran and two salamander species utilize runoff-filled wetlands adjacent to the lake. Remediation efforts in the ecosystem should include retention of isolated wetland as sources of animals for recolonization.

23807: The herpetofaunal community of a slash pine flatwoods ecosystem of north-central Florida was monitored from August 1993 through August 1994, October 1995 through September 1996, and November 1996 onward. Drift fences with funnel traps and PVC pipe refugia were used to gather baseline data on the herpetofaunal community using nine temporary ponds and the adjacent uplands, before and after a timber harvest. Study ponds ranged in size from 0.01 - 0.71 ha. Forty-five species (16 amphibian, 29 reptile) were recorded. Effects of clearcutting and site preparation included significant short-term changes in both amphibian and reptile abundance. As compared with the control, amphibian numbers were higher on the clearcut in the first two summers post-harvest (P < 0.001, P = 0.0137, respectively). Reptile numbers were higher on the clearcut in the first summer (P < 0.001). In year three (1997) for amphibians and year two (1996) for reptiles, relative abundance on the clearcut site returned to numbers comparable to those observed on the control. Movement of amphibians and reptiles was documented with distances ranging from 16 - 692 m (Mean = 98.1, n = 47, SD = 145.9). Thus some amphibians and reptiles are using large areas of the flatwoods, including upland habitat and one or more ponds.

23808: Many of Ontario's amphibian species occur in forested areas of the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence region. These species are potentially susceptible to habitat disturbance and alteration associated with selection logging protocols used to harvest uneven-aged, tolerant hardwood forests in these areas. In 1995, I began a research program to determine whether, and if so, by what mechanism(s), selection logging affects amphibian diversity and abundance at breeding sites. In 1996 and 1997, I compared amphibian abundance concurrently with habitat characteristics of: (a) 10 ephemeral breeding pools adjacent to logging roads, (b) 10 ephemeral breeding pools within forest stands logged 2-3 years prior to being surveyed, and (c) 10 ephemeral breeding pools in forest stands that had been left undisturbed for at least 30-40 years. Results of nocturnal, time constrained surveys of breeding adult abundance at these pools suggest that selection logging does not affect the abundance of breeding adults as a group. However, when I analyzed data for each species separately, I found that although selection logging does not appear to affect the relative abundance of Spring Peepers, Wood Frogs appear to be more abundant in undisturbed forests than in logged forests during the early part of the breeding season. The relative abundance of American Toads was consistently higher in breeding pools within logged forests. Stepwise multiple regression analysis suggests that variation in amphibian abundance can be explained best by variation in the duration of these ephemeral pools.

23809: The jargon of statistical power has invaded the vocabulary of almost every conservation biologist despite being largely absent from the literature as applied methodology. With respect to amphibian population monitoring, power refers to the probability of correctly rejecting the null hypothesis (that there is no decline) when the alternative hypothesis is true (a decline is occurring). Clearly we want high power in our monitoring programs so as to minimize the chance of making a Type II error (i.e., failing to detect a decline that is occurring). However, many amphibian monitoring programs likely do not have the necessary power to satisfactorily reduce the possibility that actual declines are occurring, even though some studies suggest stability and have data-sets that exceed 10 years. Here, we review the concepts of statistical power as they apply to detecting population declines. We then calculate an estimate of power for long-term data on bullfrogs (Rana catesbeiana) and wood frogs (Rana sylvatica) to investigate the problems associated with maximizing power in amphibian monitoring programs. We also comment on how an understanding of power should influence both the design of monitoring programs and management expectations.

23810: Previous amphibian relocation, repatriation, and translocation programs have proven most successful when introducing individuals in early developmental stages. Over the next 2 years, we will introduce egg masses of target amphibian species into artificial ponds in mitigated and existing wetland areas at Rocky Gap State Park. Three pairs of constructed ponds (approximately 18.5 m2) are arranged so one shallow pond (< .4m in depth) and one deep pond (> .45m in depth) comprise each pair. The shallow ponds will facilitate establishment of small, less abundant anuran species by excluding larger species with longer developmental stages. To monitor migration all ponds are encircled by drift fencing with both pitfall and funnel traps. Introduced egg masses will be monitored by recording percent hatching success and larvae will be monitored by tracking tadpole survivorship via weekly population estimates using a quadrat box sampling technique. Metamorphosed individuals captured while dispersing from the ponds will be marked with toe-clipping to determine if they return to breed in subsequent seasons. Additional marking schemes include freeze branding metamorphosed salamanders and photoidentification of anurans. Additional constructed ponds in adjacent areas are being monitored for unaided colonization.

23811: Forming a large eastern embayment on Lake Huron, Georgian Bay comprises a body of water approximately the same size as the state of Vermont. Bounded in the west by the limestone arc of the Niagara escarpment, and in the east by the Canadian Shield, the Bay encompasses some of Ontario's most spectacular scenery. It is also one of the province's richest areas for amphibians and reptiles, with 35 species recorded. In Georgian Bay Islands National Park, Beausoleil Island alone, at an area of 1100 ha, supports 32 species. Among the resident herpetofauna are the regionally rare Spotted Turtle, Eastern Hognose Snake, Eastern Fox Snake and Eastern Massasauga. During the summers of 1995 and 1996, herpetofaunal surveys were conducted on 43 of the approximately 30,000 islands in Georgian Bay. This talk will provide an overview of the varied habitats and herpetofauna of this region, as well as a discussion of the biogeographic points of interest.

23812: As consumers of 60-99% of reef primary productivity, herbivorous fishes occupy a pivotal role in channeling energy along the reef food chain. I examined feeding physiology and ecology of two territorial herbivorous damselfishes commonly found among the coral reefs of the San Blas Archipelago, Republic of Panama. I measured gut length, gut retention time, and total and nutrient-specific assimilation efficiencies and made interspecific comparisons between the dusky damselfish (S. dorsopunicans) and the threespot damselfish (S. planifrons). Relative gut length is significantly different between the two damselfish species. Dusky damselfish have a relative gut length ratio (gut length/standard length) of 1.20 and a Zihler index ((gut length/(weight^1/3)) of 3.42. Values for the threespot damselfish are 3.01 and 8.24 respectively. Despite striking differences in RGL and ZI, the gut retention time is the same for both species. Additionally, only protein assimilation efficiency (and thus total assimilation efficiency) varies between species; significantly more protein is assimilated by the threespot damselfish than the dusky damselfish. These results have several important implications. First, as both species feed on the same algal diet, the greater assimilation efficiency of the threespot damselfish may translate into faster growth rates and greater reproductive capacity. Second, it has long been held that relative gut length ratios of herbivorous fishes fall between 2 and 21, with most herbivorous damselfishes in the range of 5. The significantly lower relative gut length of dusky damselfish, unquestionably an herbivore, challenges trophic classifications based on relative gut length ratios. Third, gut morphologies are often used in phylogenetic analyses. These two damselfish are closely related congeners yet their gut morphologies vary significantly. This questions the applicability of such characters in phylogenetic analyses.

23813: Prior to 1991, the sabine shiner, Notropis sabinae, was known only from drainages west of the Mississippi River. In the process of describing the Yazoo shiner, N. rafinesquei, Suttkus noted the presence of N. sabinae within the Yazoo River, a system which lies east of the Mississippi River. Further sampling uncovered yet another eastern population within the Big Black River system. Upon preliminary examination, the latter population appears to show morphological novelties for this group. Given the diversity exhibited among populations of N. sabinae, a genetic data set was assembled to aid in defining operational taxonomic units (OTUs, sensu Mayden and Wood, 1995) within this species, and to suggest avenues for further study. Sequences were collected from the mitochondrial cytochrome b gene from individuals representing the geographic range of this species and were subjected to phylogenetic and population-level analyses. In all analyses, the Big Black River population was strongly supported as monophyletic and distinct from any other population.

23814: Identification of ichthyoplankton (eggs, larvae, and juveniles) can be a challenging task due to their small sizes and dynamic development. This problem is particularly acute for tropical and subtropical ichthyoplankton, most of which can be identified to family-level only. As part of a broader initiative to develop molecular markers for tropical and subtropical fish identification, we report on the utility of mitochondrial ribosomal gene sequences for triggerfish species identification. A 1,510 bp fragment, containing portions of the mitochondrial ribosomal genes (12S, 16S) and the complete tRNA valine gene, was sequenced from six triggerfish species (4 genera) inhabiting the western central Atlantic Ocean. Forty-three sequences were examined to assess intra- and interspecific variation. Intraspecific differences were minor (less than 0.5%); however, sufficient interspecific differences occur within this locus to allow the design of robust species-specific PCR primers. When tested in a multiplex PCR assay, these primers yielded species-diagnostic size fragments that unambiguously identified all 4 genera and 4 of the 6 species. Distinction between the two Canthidermis congeners (0.9% interspecific variation) was not possible using this approach; however, these congeners were readily distinguished using RFLP analysis of the PCR amplicon. We suggest that molecular genetic approaches can provide a robust and rapid method to tackle long-standing problems in the identification of fish species.

23815: The family Goodeidae is a distinct North American lineage of freshwater fishes and is comprised of two monophyletic subfamilies (Empetrichthyinae and Goodeinae). Empetrichthyinae contains all egg-laying species and Goodeinae contains all viviparous species. The Goodeinae is recognized as a monophyletic group based on the presence of unique morphological traits associated with internal fertilization and viviparity. The classification of goodeids has been based largely on variation of reproductive and trophic characters. A molecular phylogenetic hypothesis is presented based on the cladistic analysis of mtDNA (portions of the 16s rRNA, control region, and cytochrome b genes) and nDNA (a portion of the tyrosine kinase X-src gene) of representative goodeid fishes. The comparative method based on the molecular phylogeny was used to reconstruct the evolution of key characters traditionally used in the classification of the group such as: trophotaeniae (external projections of the embryonic gut that absorb maternal nutrients), karyotypes, and tooth and jaw structures. The phylogeny agrees with some but not all conclusions from earlier studies regarding phylogenetic relationships and reproductive and trophic character evolution.

23816: Mixing gene pools may cause outbreeding depression (OD). However, it is unknown what kind and degree of between-mate dissimilarity should exist for OD to occur. The Optimum Outbreeding Paradigm (OOP) predicts inbreeding depression (ID) for offspring of close relatives. As similarities between mates decrease, offspring fitness increases, reaches an optimal level and then decreases to levels below parental fitness (i.e., OD occurs). Populations of eastern mosquitofish (Gambusia holbrooki: Poeciliidae) from the Piedmont and Coastal Plain of two drainages were used as sources of fish for seven crosses and six pure controls each replicated in four mesocosms. OD occurred in populations of some crosses between fish from different regions and/or drainages. There were significantly more extinct populations among those founded with fish from the same vs. different region/drainage sections (7 of 20 vs. 3 of 32). Population size and growth rate, fecundity and juvenile survival were significantly lower for populations of crosses of fish from different regions and/or drainages than for those of their controls. I examined potential predictors of OD and the per-locus number of unshared alleles (Nu) between sources was the best predictor under the OOP. Optimum outcrossing and OD are expected when Nu = 0.25 and >0.45, respectively.

23817: Long bones are the major skeletal elements of vertebrate appendages. The radiations of many vertebrate clades were facilitated by locomotory innovations involving these elements (e.g. the terrestrial diversification of tetrapods) and thus it is necessary to understand how these elements changed biomechanically to more fully understand vertebrate evolution. Biomechanical attributes of long bones such as strength, modulus, and loading conditions are well documented in avian and mammalian taxa. However, data for taxa from outgroup clades are virtually non-existent and the results from the few studies that have been conducted are not in accord with those obtained for bird and mammal bones. In order to provide a better understanding of skeletal evolution, I conducted a series of biomechanical tests on long bones from a diversity of fish, amphibians, and reptiles that possessed basal locomotory attributes within their respective clades. Evolutionary trends were assessed using phylogenetic character analysis. The results suggest: 1) material properties (strength, modulus, and failure strain) did not vary throughout evolution, 2) in vivo strain regimes increased independently in birds and mammals, 3) the capacity of long bones to functionally adapt is a plesiomorphic osteichthyan trait, and 4) size and shape changes were the primary means by which long bones changed to meet evolutionary locomotory challenges.

23818: Locomotion in stingrays occurs as waves are propagated along their broadly expanded pectoral fins and can range from being undulatory to oscillatory. This study compares swimming behavior in three stingray species (Taeniura lymma, Dasyatis americana, D. sabina) differing in fin design (disc shape) as measured by aspect ratio (AR). Three-dimensional video recordings captured swimming kinematics over a range of velocities for the three species. Results indicate that D. americana (highest AR) has a significantly lower wing beat frequency and lower number of waves than the other two species. Wing amplitude, as a percentage of wing span, differs significantly in T. lymma (highest) and D. sabina (lowest). The results of frequency and number of waves corroborate previous studies suggesting that higher aspect ratio fins tend to have a lower frequency and lower number of waves than low aspect ratio fins; however, the amplitude data does not fit the prediction of high AR fins having greater amplitude. 23819: The ocular lens of fishes contains mycosporine-like amino acids (MAAs), which attenuate short wavelengths of light.
