23934: Timing of physiological changes associated with the parr-smolt transformation has been intimately linked with changes in photoperiod and temperature. However, there is little direct evidence concerning environmental control of downstream migratory behavior. Seasonal timing of physiological and behavioral changes associated with increased temperatures was examined. Atlantic salmon parr and pre-smolts were tagged with passive integrated transponders (PIT) in March, placed in simulated stream conditions and monitored continuously from April through July. Water temperature was increased 1°C every 3 d (ambient), 1°C every other day (advanced), or 1°C every 9 d (delayed). The number of downstream passages of smolts peaked in May. Downstream movements of parr were two-orders of magnitude lower than of smolts. Fish maintained under ambient and advanced conditions ceased activity by mid-June. Fish exposed to the delayed temperature regime sustained downstream movements through July. In late June gill Na+, K+ -ATPase activity (an index of osmoregulatory physiology) had decreased in smolts maintained under ambient and advanced regimes, whereas it remained elevated in the delayed group. Temperature regimes dramatically affect smolt physiology, behavior, and migratory timing. Fluctuating water temperature and its influence on migration must be considered when contemplating survival of hatchery and wild smolts to the marine stage.

23935: Osmoregulatory abilities of American shad must be coordinated with migrations between fresh water (FW) and seawater (SW). Shad develop the ability to tolerate SW at larval-juvenile transition (26-45 d post-hatch) coincident with 3.5 and 10-fold increases in chloride cell (CC) number and gill Na+,K+-ATPase activity respectively. Although only early development is limited to low salinities, shad remain in FW for 5-6 months (until autumn). During autumnal migration juveniles lose the ability to osmoregulate in FW, evidenced by a decline in plasma chloride (20%). Shad kept in the laboratory through Dec. experience large declines in plasma chloride (68%) and high mortality. Gill Na+,K+-ATPase activity increases 3-fold and gill CC's on the primary and secondary lamellae increase 2-fold and 1.5-fold; these are likely to be compensatory mechanisms for increasing ion uptake. Changes in plasma chloride, gill Na+,K+-ATPase, and CC's are reduced and delayed if shad are maintained at 24°C versus a natural decline in temperature. Impaired osmoregulatory ability, as influenced by temperature, may serve as a proximate cue for migration. Changes in temperature (e.g. global warming) will likely alter the timing of migration.

23936: To date, few studies have examined how food availability may constrain the reproduction, growth and mortality of coral reef fishes in their natural habitat. To address this issue, we compared the life history tactics of supplementally fed, wild, adult beaugregory damselfish (Stegastes leucostictus) with those of control fish during a series of 90-day experimental trials. These herbivorous fish showed both seasonal and lunar patterns of reproduction in the study area off the coast of Panama. During the study, patterns of reproductive output and growth of control fish varied temporally and spatially, apparently in response to natural patterns of food availability. Growth rates, though variable, did not correspond well with levels of reproductive output. Mortality was generally high, though somewhat reduced during periods of low reproduction. Protein rich food supplements greatly increased reproduction and growth of experimental fish and substantially lowered rates of mortality, irrespective of season. These results strongly suggest that food limitation plays a critical role in determining both the seasonal timing and intensity of reproduction, growth, and mortality in this species.

23937: Among salmonines (trout, salmon, char), there is a consistent trend for large females to spawn before small ones within a breeding season. This pattern may be related to competition for limited spawning sites or, alternatively, small females may delay reproduction as an adaptive tactic to minimise brood loss. Females routinely lose broods through the subsequent use of nest sites by other females. Broods of small females are more likely to be lost by this disturbance because nest depth is related to body size. We tested these alternative hypotheses by detaining the largest females in a marked population of lake-spawning brook trout (Salvelinus fontinalis). The competition hypothesis predicts small females would breed earlier in the absence of large females, whereas the adaptive tactic hypothesis predicts delayed breeding. Consistent with our second hypothesis, small females spawned significantly later during the experimental year (1996) compared to the previous two years. Furthermore, brood loss was significantly reduced. Within seasons, brood loss was significantly higher for small than large females. Site choice may also play an important role in reproductive success. We show that small females increase reproductive success by delayed reproduction and suggest that this adaptive tactic may be socially mediated.

23938: Size-dependent asynchrony in the seasonal timing of reproduction has been well documented for fish in temperate regions. A common explanation of this phenomenon is that small fish are physiologically forced to postpone the allocation of energy to reproduction, resulting in a delay in the seasonal timing of reproductive activity. However, for male fathead minnows we suggest that the timing of seasonal reproductive activity is regulated by social interactions. In an enclosure and a pond experiment, small males advanced their reproductive condition, held nesting territories, and spawned only when isolated from large males or once large males were removed from the population. Small males were of similar size in all experimental treatments, suggesting that size-dependent differences in energy allocation do not account for differences in their phenology. Preliminary analyses also indicate that the production and size of young produced by small 'uninhibited' males was not significantly different from the production and size of young produced by large dominant males. Thus, the release of small males from social control may expedite population recovery following a size-dependent disturbance such as winterkill.

23939: Marbled salamanders (Ambystoma opacum) inhabit woodlands throughout much of the eastern United States. Adults typically migrate to temporary pond breeding sites en masse in early autumn, where courtship, breeding, and terrestrial oviposition occur over a 3-4 week period. Energetically "spent" adults leave the site with virtually all lipid stores depleted. Experimental manipulations of food level suggest that adult reproductive frequency is dependent on prior food acquisition; thus food availability in the terrestrial habitat may partly explain the wide among-individual variation in year-to-year breeding patterns. Larval success is highly dependent on the timing of pond filling and drying: hydroperiod directly affects mortality and strongly influences competitive and predatory interactions. Per-capita food resources in the larval stage determine larval growth rates, larval period, body size at metamorphosis, and a suite of post-metamorphic adult traits. Although variation in larval period can be substantial, there is surprisingly little variation in the absolute date of metamorphosis. Larvae from eggs hatched 3-mo apart generally metamorphose within a few weeks of each other, regardless of whether the aquatic habitat remains suitable for growth. Later-hatching larvae therefore metamorphose at a smaller size in spite of the strong relationship between body size at metamorphosis and traits related to adult fitness. Food resources available to individuals in both the aquatic and terrestrial stages of the life cycle affect the resource allocation "decisions" a salamander makes. Understanding allocation decisions is critical to modeling the population dynamics of Ambystoma opacum.

23940: Variation in abiotic parameters determines the timing of reproduction in many semi-aquatic amphibians; hence, the timing of first reproduction is constrained by extrinsic (e.g., temperature and rainfall) rather than intrinsic (e.g., the rate of gametogenesis) factors. Adaptations that release organisms from extrinsic factors may have important individual- and population-level implications. We describe the pattern of metamorphosis and maturation in natural and experimental populations of the salamander Ambystoma talpoideum. Prior to first reproduction (usually at 1-yr post-hatching), individuals that metamorphose are sexually immature when leaving the aquatic environment, and must mature in the terrestrial environment. Maturation, however, may precede metamorphosis. Individuals that mature prior to metamorphosis remain in the aquatic environment (i.e., become "paedomorphic"), are physiologically capable of breeding at the start of the breeding season, in the early fall. Terrestrial adults, however, must wait for the proper suite of environmental conditions to initiate migration to the aquatic breeding habitats, which may be delayed until mid to late winter. The result is a potentially large difference in the timing of reproduction between the two morphs. The consequences of differential maturation and reproduction among individuals may collectively have larger population-level effects.

23941: The corn snake, northern pine snake, and eastern king snake reach the northern limit of their range in the Pine Barrens of southern New Jersey. 23942: Painted turtles (Chrysemys picta) hatch in late summer but usually remain in the nest during winter. Hatchlings can survive subzero temperatures in the nest either by tolerating the freezing of their body tissues, at temperatures to -4 °C, or by avoiding ice nucleation and remaining supercooled (unfrozen) to temperatures at least as low as -12 °C. We investigated the effects of soil composition and soil moisture on susceptibility to ice inoculation in hatchling turtles endemic to the sandhills of Nebraska, where soil moisture in winter is variable (range 4-14%). Turtles cooled in frozen, native soil (predominantly sand) froze at -1.6 °C, whereas turtles cooled in frozen soil to which clay or peat was added supercooled to -13 °C before freezing. Avoidance of inoculation by environmental ice in turtles exposed to frozen native soil was possible only when the soil contained little moisture (<4%). Thus, survival of relatively low nest temperatures, by supercooling, may be greater for turtles hibernating in sandy soils containing little moisture, or in soils containing clay or organic matter. However, the winter microenvironment contains numerous ice nuclei (e.g., inorganic particulates, microorganisms) that may nevertheless promote inoculative freezing.

23943: Although studies of body temperature (Tb) are extensive for snakes living in temperate regions, few studies have focused on tropical, nocturnal snakes. 23944: In the highly seasonal environments of the north temperate zone, ectothermic animals such as snakes suffer significant temporal constraints on their annual cycles, with consequences for their life histories and demographies. For example, cold winters prohibit any activity at all, but summers also may be cool, further restricting activity. In presumed evolutionary response to this, most temperate-zone snakes are viviparous; gravid females exhibit precise behavioural thermoregulation, apparently providing optimal developmental conditions for their young. However, thermoregulation often conflicts with other activities such as feeding. In fact, in many species, gravid females feed little or not at all, even in captivity. The main demographic consequences of this are reduced future reproductive output, especially through decreased reproductive frequency of individual females. Nonetheless, this tradeoff may be relatively unimportant in the long run because many snakes are long-lived "bet-hedging" species and compensate for low reproductive output in one year by surviving to reproduce at a later date. I illustrate these ideas with data for garter snakes (Thamnophis) and rattlesnakes (Crotalus).

23947: Studies on north temperate fish species indicate that new habitat availability following the last glacial retreat has promoted ecological speciation in post-glacial lakes. The extensive ecophenotypic polymorphism observed among Great Lakes ciscoes suggests that they have radiated through trophic adaptation and reproductive isolation. 23975: We used DNA sampled from black rat snakes (Elaphe o. obsoleta) and eastern massasauga rattlesnakes (Sistrurus c. catenatus) in Ontario to investigate genetic population structure at several spatial scales. 23979: Recent geological, paleontological, morphological, and molecular studies provide identification and better definitions of the diverse clades that comprise the present American snake fauna. No single field provides a clear zoogeographic narrative of these faunal elements but the consilience of information from multiple sources offers such a base. Not unexpectedly, the oldest surviving clades are also the most ancient ones in the Americas. The typhlopids and leptotyphlopids of the Neotropics and Africa probably date from the mid-Cretaceous splitting of Gondwana by the Atlantic Ocean. The anomalepedids and Anilius in contrast are ancient South American endemics without known relatives, although the latter may be a Recent relative of the Cretaceous +Dinilysia. The Neotropical (true) boids appear to represent an ancient henophidian fauna that ranged from Madagascar across Antarctica to South America. Conversely, the American erycids, tropidophiids (and ?ungaliophiids and ?Loxocemus) derive from the Cretaceous-to-Eocene connection of eastern North America with Europe. This also may be true of the caenophidian "North American Relicts." The main American caenophidian fauna (crotalids, elapids, xenodontids, dipsadids, colubrids s.s., and natricids) did not arrive until later. 23998: We sampled the ichthyofauna of the Upper Jurua Extractive Reserve (Brazilian Amazon) through gillnet fishing, in the main upper Jurua river, its tributaries and the floodplain lakes in the wet and dry seasons. The dry season yielded a greater number, biomass, species richness and diversity of fishes than the wet period, what can be due the concentration of fishes due to low water level. The diversity and species richness do not varied between habitats, but the lakes yielded a greater biomass of fish than the main river and tributaries. This could be associated to a greater stability of the lakes, less subjected to subtle variations in water level. The fish assemblages varied mainly between the two seasons and between lakes and the lothic environments. This spatial variation was more pronounced during the dry season (when lakes and rivers showed a more distinct ichthyofauna). In the wet season there was a certain mixing in fish composition among the habitats, probably due to dispersal movements effectuated by the fishes in the innundated forest. We observed a high total fish diversity in the Upper Jurua River, what can be related partially to a high beta diversity, or variation in species composition between habitats.

23999: Seasonal movements of the porbeagle shark, Lamna nasus, in Canadian Atlantic waters were determined using size and sex composition of catches sampled by Fisheries Observers in the porbeagle longline fishery. Males and immature females predominate porbeagle catches on the Scotian Shelf edge in March and April. The data suggest that mature females segregate from the main body of the population during this period. The proportion of mature females in catches increases in May and June. Porbeagle move onto the Shelf in May and northeastward along the Shelf in May and June, moving into the Gulf of St. Lawrence and onto the Grand Banks in late June and early July. Larger porbeagle move off the Shelf into the Gulf of St. Lawrence and onto the Grand Banks first, followed by younger porbeagle. Large porbeagle begin to leave the Gulf in September and large females predominate catches on the Grand Banks in September to November. Porbeagle move out of the Gulf and off the Grand Banks in November and out to the Shelf edge in December. Migration of the porbeagle shark in Canadian Atlantic waters is complex and catch rate analyses should incorporate size and sex composition of catches on a seasonal basis.
